utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Monday. Let me first greet the witness, Mr. Filipovic. Good afternoon to the accused who are present. Good afternoon to the Defence counsel, to Mr. Scott and his team, and all the people assisting us. We are going to continue with the cross-examination. Mr. Scott, I believe you have one hour and thirty minutes left. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel, all those in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Filipovic. Sir, I'd like to finish with the topic that we were about to close on Thursday afternoon. There was a pending question and then a substantial amount of discussion among the lawyers in the court. But the pending question to you at that time in connection with Exhibit P11131, and I don't think it's necessary to turn there, it is the BBC article of a Croatian new agency report. It's the one that we talked about on Friday -- excuse me, Thursday, where the last statement that was attributed to you and that was pending at the time was a statement that you had made to this effect: "To me, this is the third aggression [following Serbian and Muslim] against Croats in Central Bosnia. This one is being conducted by the international community." The question that I put to you and was pending at the time that we finished on Thursday was: "That was your view at the time, that was your view, sir, when you came to testify in the Kordic case, and that's your view today, isn't it?"

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have given a great many interviews. I don't know whether it was properly conveyed. I'm not quite sure I said "the third aggression against the Croats." But knowing Ivica Santic, that is to say, the accused, and knowing Pero Skopljak, another accused, as far as I was concerned at that time, and ultimately Aleksovski, too, Blaskic, Kordic, and I don't know who else -- anyway, it was a bit strange that the first indictments to be raised for the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina [realtime transcript read in error "Republic of Herceg-Bosna"] were raised for a defence which was the purest defence that you could imagine; that is to say, for people to defend themselves from an aggression and so on. So as I say, I'm not sure I used that word, and to the present day I would not refrain from terms and expressions when it comes to a group of accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have an intervention to the transcript. In line 25 on the second page, it was recorded that the witness said that this was the first indictment to be raised for the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, but he said "Bosnia and Herzegovina." And I wanted to put that right, "Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, you say that this involved what you called here "the purest defence," but of course the Chamber will have in mind the conclusions of this Tribunal in the Kordic case, the Blaskic case, the Aleksovski case, and the Cerkez case, which may not have painted the same picture that you've attempted to paint. You understand that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am talking about what I experienced, what I lived through for three and a half years. I'm talking about a period of eight months in a closed area, where not even a bird could fly in, an area that we defended, and we defended exclusively the Croats. It was an area which could be targeted by the Muslims. They could target each other, shoot at each other, so that the defence was crystal clear, as pure as the driven snow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let's move forward to the role of the HVO in the structure of what was happening during the events -- during this time, excuse me. A number of questions were put to you in that regard by Ms. Alaburic. Let's start with just some very basic facts. The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised as a sovereign, independent state by the European Community on 6th April, 1992, and by the United States the following day on 7 April 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Just one moment, please. Your Honours, again we have a problem with the record on page 22, 23, where it says -- what it says there is quite unclear. The witness uttered a sentence which it is difficult to translate. I understood what it was about. Perhaps the best thing would be to have the witness repeat. The witness said that the Muslim forces or Muslim soldiers could -- and he used the word "prostrijeliti," and in that way "kill each," so perhaps the witness could explain what he means by the word "prostrijeliti," because this as it stands is not clear. I think that would be a good idea, if the witness were to explain exactly what he meant. Otherwise, we're not going to understand the translation as it stands.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can repeat. An enclave, the Lasva Valley that was defending itself, was so small, so narrow, that the Muslims on the one side could shoot at the Muslims on the other side, so in that sense it was an entrance/exit sort of wound or passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The question I had put to you, and which I'll now have to take the time to put again: You would agree, sir, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised as a sovereign, independent state by the European Community on 6th April, 1992, and by the United States the following day on the 7th April of 1992; you have no reason to disagree with that, do you?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was proud that Bosnia and Herzegovina had been recognised as a state and that I am today a general of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, further, the new independent, sovereign state had an internationally-recognised legal government in the BiH Presidency and the BiH Government, and had sovereign, internationally-recognised territory extending to all its international borders, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as a professional soldier, it would hardly be surprising to you, would it, sir, that the new government of this new sovereign state took immediate steps to establish its armed forces?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the international community recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina, the territory and the government, that was one thing, and the people that lived there was the Serbs, the Croats, and the Muslims. But as far as the question goes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you're aware, aren't you, at least generally, that on the 8th of April, 1992, the BiH Presidency abolished the old Territorial Defence under the former JNA system and put a new Territorial Defence in place, which then some weeks later became the ABiH or Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact dates, but I did know the commander. Efendic was his name. I knew him personally, and he was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That really wasn't my question, sir, and I'll ask you to please co-operate with me so that we can use our time today as efficiently as possible. You knew, sir, that immediately, essentially, on becoming a new state, the government of that new state of Bosnia-Herzegovina took steps to establish its armed forces, which were originally known as the Territorial Defence, a new Territorial Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about that, and I couldn't know about that. What I did know was that measures were being taken to defend the country because a pressure was exerted against it in the form of an aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you turn, please, to Exhibit 155, P00155. We're going to look at two exhibits fairly quickly, and then I'm going to put some questions to you. P00155, 155. Can we have the assistance of the usher, please. 155. If you'll look at that just to acquaint yourself with it. And the Chamber has seen this and the next two documents a number of times. I'm not going to spend a great deal of time on them. This is an order issued by Mate Boban on the 10th of April, 1992, among other things declaring that the HVO military was the only legal armed force on the territory of Herceg-Bosna. If you will look next, please, at P00195. It should be very close following the one you were just looking at, P00195. This was a very similar order, I put to you, for those who may have time, if they haven't already done so, to compare the text from Colonel General Ante Roso on the 8th of May, 1992, again saying at number 1: "The only legal military units in the territory of the HZ-HB are units of the HVO." Then I'll next ask you to turn, please, to P00200, which I again think will be very close, P00200. And likewise, sir, I would explain this document to you as an order by General Blaskic, or Colonel Blaskic at the time, dated the 11th of May, 1992, referring by number to Mr. Roso's order and essentially ordering on down the line, so to speak, again number 1: "The only legal military units in the area of Kiseljak municipality are HVO units," et cetera. Now, starting with Mr. Boban's order of the 10th of April, 1992, can you explain to the Chamber any legal basis that Mr. Boban had to issue such an order?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection to this question. This is a legal issue, and I don't think that it's a proper question for an officer to be asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Blaskic at this time was under my command. That is to say, I was in the Lasva Valley and he was in Kiseljak, and he issued this order, and I assume that it reached him, although I don't know how. But I didn't receive an order of this kind, nor did I hand it down to my subordinates, although at the time I was the commander of the Regional Staff of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It doesn't really answer my question, sir. You're a senior commander. In fact, you just told us at the moment you were the senior commander. You surely must have had some idea on the basis on which you were exercising command. On what basis was the HVO military command, under the leadership of Mate Boban, asserting at this time that the HVO was the only legal military force?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Central Bosnia, full command of the Regional Staff, it wasn't Boban or Roso who appointed me. It was the situation in which I imposed myself as commander. Why? Well, from the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, papers would go around, but what I had, my inalienable right, then and at all times, was to defend people, the population at that point in time, and to organise them as best as possible, and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. [Interpretation] I'm going to have to ask the witness to slow down, because half of what he said has not been interpreted. So could he repeat that answer to this question, to speak slower, because I'm sure the interpreters will become very tired before the end of today's session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's probably my temperament, and maybe it's the pressure on me all the time to ask me to confirm something. He says I must confirm something all the time. I'm being asked to confirm. So I had to know, I had to take steps, and throughout the time I did take steps. I did what I had to do in order to defend the people, the population, the area in Central Bosnia. The papers that arrived or that were sent off was something I wasn't interested in. I was interested in reality, the situation on the ground. Let me repeat, I wasn't appointed by Boban, or Roso, or anybody, nor did I see any of these papers. It was a meeting of the municipalities of Central Bosnia at which there were 12 municipalities represented, because after that time Asko [phoen] was the commander, but it was decided that I should be the commander at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down please, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That may or may not have been true in the first couple of days, but you know full well that within a matter of days you were part of a structure called the HVO, you had certain positions -- you were given certain positions, Blaskic was appointed to certain positions, and you know full well that was done pursuant to a structure that was then referred to as the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the structure of the HVO. Blaskic arrived there 20 days after me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's look at Mr. Roso's order, in particular, for a moment, item number -- P00195, item number 2: "All other military units in the above territory must join the single defence system." Now, why was that? What would be the purpose of Mr. Roso saying all military units on the territory of the HZ-HB must join the single defence system?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there were operations towards the HVO, in the sense that it was illegal and didn't exist. Now, I personally was contacted by the commander of the Territorial Defence Staff of Zenica, in which -- well, on day 10 he said I was illegal, so he was legal and I was illegal. I was at the front, establishing the front-line, whereas he was sitting in Zenica. So this legal/illegal, lawful/unlawful, was a game that was played all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You didn't answer my question, sir. Please, I would appreciate your co-operation. Please listen to my question. Roso says: "All other military units in the above territory must join the single defence system." Why? Why must they all join the single defence system?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They accepted me as commander in the Lasva Valley in the first few months of the war, into a united system of defence, because it couldn't have been otherwise. So the Territorial Defence, that is to say, people there in the field, and at the beginning, when the Mujahedin arrived as well, they tolerated me and accepted me. It was a united system of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why did Roso say that all military units on the territory of Herceg-Bosna had to recognise the HVO Main Staff as their "supreme command"?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'd have to ask him that, because you're asking me this for the fourth time already, and I am telling you that there was a united defence system. To establish a defence system, why united? Because in the area there were units, weapons, people, and the structure of defence -- well, the armature was the HVO and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we established last week and you still agree, don't you, that the supreme commander of the HVO was the president of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So why would you say, sir -- why did Mr. Roso say, your superior at this time -- and you said very clearly a few moments ago you were accused of being an illegal -- part of an illegal military force. Why is it that Roso would say that any military units on the territory of Herceg-Bosna had to recognise essentially, in so many words, Mate Boban as their supreme commander?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know what territory of Herceg-Bosna this was. It was never defined, although at least not to my knowledge. Secondly, why Roso? I didn't know Roso at all, so as I say, I didn't know him. And, thirdly, let me repeat, action gives rise to reaction, and the action was that the -- only the Territorial Defence was the sole force, and everything had to be subservient to that, and then this gave rise to a reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So let me put it to you this way, sir: In Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time, in April/May 1993, who was the supreme commander, Mate Boban or the BiH Presidency?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the Lasva Valley, it was me, and nobody in between, in the sense of arriving, an order arriving, information arriving, weapons arriving, or anything linked to the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Roso's order number 3 says: "Every member of the above military units must wear HVO insignia ..." You were familiar with that, weren't you, as the practice, as the required practice?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only later that we managed to sew on the insignia and put them on the members of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, on the 8th of May, 1992, Ante Roso ordered every member of the above military units -- all legal units, according to him, on the territory of Herceg-Bosna were required to wear HVO insignia. Now, did you not testify in the Kordic case that the HVO insignia was "the insignia of the Croatian people"?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The insignia of the Croatian Defence Council and the Croatian people. And not only the people, but the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please, what steps, in April, May, June, July 1992, the HVO armed forces took to place themselves under the command of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its presidency?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forces of the Croatian Defence Council were a function of the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's not my question. You keep saying that, but tell me the specific steps that the HVO armed forces took in April, May, June, July 1992 to put themselves under the command of the BiH Presidency of the sovereign state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Tell me specific steps that the HVO took to do that.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we undertook to do was that in the units and the area, we took in all the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the people from Krajina, the refugees that were pouring in. We've already heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What steps did you take, sir, to put yourself under the command of the BiH Presidency, the HVO? It has nothing to do with taking in the population of the Krajina. What steps did you take -- did the HVO take to put themselves under the command and control of the BiH Presidency? It's a very simple and clear question.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very clear that I didn't take a single step to place myself under the command of somebody who cannot command, that doesn't have the infrastructure to do so, somebody that doesn't have a built-up system for that, for everything to function properly. I didn't take a single step in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, sir, you knew full well -- you and the other HVO senior commanders around you knew full well that the HVO had no intention, at the time or after that time, to become a genuine part of a single unified system under the command of the Bosnian Presidency? You had no such intention ever, did you?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today, in 1999 [as interpreted], that's what you say. We knew nothing else but to survive. That's all we knew, how to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you're doing yourself a disservice. You're an educated man, a professional officer. You know what I'm asking you, and you're avoiding the question. I've asked you very specifically. You said you were fighting for Bosnia-Herzegovina. You said that -- a number of things that you've said, that, We were all part of the same thing. And I'm putting to you, sir, you knew full well at the time you had no intentions of genuinely putting yourself under the command of the BiH Presidency. Now, that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, in the command, the regional Staff in Vitez, the president, a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Boras, I think he was, at least -- Boras, yes, he arrived, and in talking to him I didn't gain the impression that I was illegal in any way and that I shouldn't be doing what I was doing. Quite the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the demands of the BiH government at the time, the documents that the Judges have seen before, are very similar, really, in fact, to what Mr. Roso was saying. Mr. Roso says, All military units operating on this territory must joint a single defence system. So said the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If you're operating on our territory, the territory recognised by the international community, you must joint the single defence system. Likewise, Mr. Roso says in his view of the world, You must recognise the HVO Main Staff as your supreme command. And what the Bosnian government was saying, No, you must recognise the Bosnian government as your supreme command. Now, I put it to you, sir, the logic is the same, but you can't have it both ways, you cannot serve two masters. There's one supreme commander, and the HVO had no intention of submitting itself to the command of the BiH Government, did it?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this something that the Prosecutor is claiming, Why does this element, Herceg-Bosna or Bosna-Herzegovina -- why couldn't it be Bosnia and Herzegovina? Everything that the Prosecutor is saying now is the kind of thinking that somebody else had outside the territory in which we were active.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you know exactly what I'm asking you because you were essentially asked the same question by Mr. Nice in the Kordic case. Mr. Nice asked you this question: "Picking up on what you said not so long ago, if you really wanted to organise defence jointly, why not have one army, why have two?" This the answer you gave, under oath, sitting in this same building some years ago: "We had three armies in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Army of Republika Srpska, which separated and took up arms to reach their objectives; then we had the Muslim side, which wore the green fezzes, had their own flags, had their own insignia; then we had the Croatian component or party and represented the interest of that side. And if you're talking about the joint defence of Croats and Bosniaks, that is, Muslims, that was jointly but not the same. At that time, we could not have had the same army. That was a purely theoretical concept." You could not have had the same army, according to your sworn testimony in the Kordic case, sir. Now, do you stand by that today?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina comprises the elements that you have just enumerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm talking about --

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back then --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, please, 1992 and 1993. Your position was and what you told another set of three Judges some years ago, under oath, was that at that time there could not possibly be one army, that each side had its own army and they could not possibly be the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing. If I could give the Prosecutor a hand, to make sure you don't keep disagreeing with the witness unnecessarily. The witness started answering the question, but the interpreters didn't have the time to interpret. If you have the time to wait up, you will see that he was, indeed, trying to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Counsel, but his question [sic] started with "today," and I'm not talking about today. Unfortunately, I wish I had more time, but as you know, we don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you know full well what I'm talking about, and it would behoove you not to play games on this. You're an educated man. You testified to the Kordic Judges that there could not be a single combined army with the Muslims; perhaps something jointly, but could not possibly have had the same army. In your words, that was a purely theoretical concept; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe I didn't go to the same school as the Prosecutor, maybe we weren't schoolmates, maybe I don't have the same words that he has, but it is me testifying here and I'm telling you exactly how it was. I'm not about to change my evidence. I said the same thing nine or ten years ago at a different trial, and I'm still saying all the same things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We'll turn next to the next couple of documents that were put in front of you on this topic of the HVO and its status in relationship to the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm not going to pull these out because of time, but I'll refer to the 20 April 1993 cease-fire agreement which was shown to you, which is Exhibit P01988, and to the 25 April 1993 joint statement by Boban and Izetbegovic in Zagreb, which was P -- or is P02078. Now, sir, both of those documents were put to you as including or containing statements about the HVO being a legitimate part of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I want to come back to that in a moment. But to tie a couple of things together, because our time is limited: You can confirm, can't you, that around the end of April you joined this joint commission that you talked about, around the 28th of April, 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you served on that commission until approximately the 10th of June, 1993, when you returned to your duties with Colonel Blaskic in Central Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have an objection based on the document that the Prosecutor is referring to. The joint command was formed, not the joint commission.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the joint command, yes, but it also operated as a separation commission. The first two or three days until the joint command was appointed --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question is, sir -- my question to you, and I'm not going to play word games with you now. My question is: You were on that commission, that body, between the 28th of April, 1993, until the 10th of June, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on that body from the 20 -- the 21st, or the 22nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as I understand it, that joint commission did not meet again after the 14th of April, 1993, because of the ongoing conflicts, including what was happening at that time in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that it did meet, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Unfortunately, sir, you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that this commission had a very, very short life span, and unfortunately at the end of the day there was no lasting peace or real improvements coming out of that commission; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It went on for a very short time, had a short life span.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And tying this back in to those two documents and the two exhibits I referred to you, sir, the 20 April cease-fire and the 25 April joint statement, isn't it simply the reality, sir, those were statements made in the course of the negotiations that ultimately didn't go anywhere and really weren't worth the pieces of paper that they were printed on?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a lot of activity about the statements and about the operation of the joint command throughout that month. Thousands of persons were freed from some sort of detention on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But ultimately within a few short days, sir, both sides were back at killing each other, that the HVO was sending Muslims to the Heliodrom camp. Basically, in a very short time, in the matter of a few days, the war continued on; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the prisons and the prisons in which Croats were detained. In Central Bosnia, Delic, Sefer and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the war continued on, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war continued, yes, in the second half of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it's a bit like -- let me put to you, perhaps, the summary of another professional soldier, such as yourself, and see if you can agree with his assessment. There was a witness in this case who was an international monitor named Bo Pellnas, and Bo Pellnas came to this courtroom, and on the question of cease-fires and how many there were, and there were so many, one cease-fires after another, and he said this in his testimony: "Well, after a while in these conditions, you know, you don't take much notice of paperwork or oral statements. You wait to see what happens. So you don't get, I would say, optimistic or pessimistic about the announcements that a cease-fire has been signed. You wait and see what happens before you make any evaluation of it." And you would agree with that statement by Mr. Pellnas, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a true professional, and his statement shows it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, in fact, in your testimony last week you really expressed the same sentiment. You said last Monday, in reference to questions put to you by Judge Antonetti on the Constitutional Court, you said: "All those documents, agreements, did not mean a thing for me, when I spent hours every day being fired at." At the end of the day, sir, what was said on paper really didn't make much difference, did it?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were negotiations throughout and combat as well going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And at the end of the April, you agree, don't you, that when the fighting broke out again and the joint commission went away, and the cease-fire agreements went away, there was fault on both sides; Croats were attacking, Muslims were attacking, there was fault on both sides, and the process simply came to an end, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would change this the other way around. The Muslims were attacking, the Croats were defending but also attacking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you testified in the Kordic case. You said: "There was a big meeting in Travnik at the end of April. Thebault was there, the European Union, others were there. The attacks did not stop, not only from the Muslim side. I repeat that, in all those incidents, because Croats were also participating in these incidents." And in another statement a few pages later, you said you couldn't lay the blame at the door of the Muslims, "but at Croats as well." Isn't that what you said in the Kordic case?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the meeting in Travnik, when Thebault was there, as soon as we were out of that room Cuskic saved me when I was facing hundreds of Muslim barrels. They wanted to kill me. Cuskic stood right in front of them, unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, there was fault on both sides. You so testified in the Kordic case on two separate occasions under oath. Are you changing your answer now?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not changing anything. I'm telling you that both sides were provoking incidents.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the last part of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The last document on the topic that I will ask you about, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Scott. The interpreter asks the witness to repeat the last sentence. He did not understand you, Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both sides were provoking incidents and clashes throughout all of this until the Washington Accords were adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Finally, sir, on this topic you were shown a transcript of a meeting of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 29th of June, 1993, and you, in the courtroom, may recall it, because right at the very beginning of the document, without any reference or quotation or any other information that contained the statement: "We recognised the HVO as a constituent part of the armed forces." The short answer on that document, sir, is you don't know anything about it, do you?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, from the very first day the HVO was part of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The moment of the recognition may have a legal significance, but de facto and de jure, on the ground the same thing continued throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, you said earlier you didn't know, because you said you weren't bothered by such things. My question to you is: You don't know anything about that document; you weren't in the meeting, you don't know what was said, none of us in the courtroom, in fact, knows what was said, we don't know who, if anyone, made that statement. We don't know what it's about, do we? Let me make it very clear. I'm talking about -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, objection, Your Honours, objection. Can Mr. Scott please give us the page number for the transcript reference. What exactly did the witness say a while ago, because it's difficult to keep going like this. It's difficult for us to monitor what is going on. We should also try to show how what the witness said in his former testimony is being misrepresented. What we have on page 5, line 5, where Mr. Scott said that the witness said something earlier, can he please specify what, when, as well as the transcript page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you, in the courtroom, know full well that Ms. Alaburic put before you a document 1D02664, which was a transcript of the meeting of the Presidency, and everyone knows -- in the courtroom knows that I'm not making that up. My point is a very simple one. That document was put in front of you, but you don't know anything about either the document or its content, did you, because you were not at that meeting and you can't tell these Judges anything about what happened at that meeting, what was said, or the outcome of that meeting; correct? It's a very simple question. You simply don't know?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the meeting or about the document. I know nothing about it. The only thing I do know is what I read in the press, in the printed media. I was also shown the document while I was being proofed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, did you read in the printed media, sir, about the Constitutional Court decision that said Herceg-Bosna was illegal? Sir?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was after the war. It was disclosed to me after the war. But while all of this was going on, I knew neither of these two things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You voiced an opinion in response to a question by counsel about whether Mr. Delic should be attending a meeting of the Presidency if Mr. Petkovic was not also attending. Were you aware, sir, that the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina during a time of war provided that the expanded Presidency included the head of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. But Delic had nothing to do at a Presidency meeting unless Petkovic was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: According to you. And can you tell us, by the way, how many meetings of the HVO Defence Department, headed by Mr. Stojic, or how many meetings of the HVO government, headed by Mr. Prlic, did any of the senior Muslim military officers attend?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: None that you know of; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really do have an objection. Of course not, he doesn't know anything about that. Of course, the Prosecutor should first lay the foundation, Did you ever attend an HVO meeting? Yes. Very well. Who was there? Were there any Muslim soldiers there? No. Okay. If not, then he can't ask any further questions. But my learned friend just breezes right through it, the witness says, No, and then he draws whatever conclusion he likes. This is entirely unfair. In a Croatian courtroom, I would be severely reprimanded for that sort of practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I haven't asked any question for 45 minutes. I let Mr. Scott freely conduct his cross-examination. But given the last questions he put to you, I would like to ask you something. I would like first the Registrar to have document 1D2664, the document mentioned by Mr. Scott, could we have this on the screen, please. We have the text in English, and could we please have it also in B/C/S. Very well, everyone has it on the screen. We have both documents. The text in B/C/S is a transcription from a tape-recording. Nobody has the tape-recording, unfortunately, but that's not where the problem lies. This is June 29, 1993, 1.30 p.m. The session is chaired by Mr. Izetbegovic, himself. Mr. Scott told you that you did not attend this meeting. Of course you didn't attend the meeting. Otherwise, your name would be listed here. But we had a great number of witnesses who came to testify on the presidential transcripts, and they did not attend these meetings either. But this being said, Witness, let's take a look at the first sentence: "We recognise the HVO as a constituent part of the armed forces." To me, I get the impression - maybe I'm wrong - but it seems that Mr. Izetbegovic is chairing the meeting and is stating this, but his name is not mentioned. Normally, his name should have been placed right before the sentence, but that's not the case here. But, well, we might assume that he is saying that. And then Pejanovic takes the floor, and we see what he says, and then the president speaks again. The president is, of course, Mr. Izetbegovic. He resumes what Pejanovic said and says, and I quote: "It says here that there is only one commander in chief of the armed forces." So to me it seems that Mr. Izetbegovic recognised that the HVO was an element of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but that according to him, there are several commanders, because Pejanovic actually took the floor right before him. General, I'm sure you're well versed in all this. You told us, you know, that you're a retired general of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So when looking at this document, could you tell us whether Mr. Izetbegovic officially told all members of the meeting that according to him, the HVO was a constituent part of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Excuse me, Your Honour. I know it's -- I know it's not exactly customary, but that's exactly the point of my question to this witness. He can't possibly speculate to who said that. It doesn't say on the record. The witness has said he wasn't there. He can't possibly say, nor can the courtroom possibly say, who said [indiscernible] or made this statement. It's pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, it is speculation, yes, but when you're telling the witness that he is speculating, I'm not speculating, myself. I have a document here on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It doesn't say who made that statement, sir. It does not say anything about who made that statement. Anyone drawing that conclusion is purely speculating, anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, I said that regarding the first sentence, we don't know who uttered these words. It's true, and Mr. Scott has pressed that point. But when reading the document, it seems that there is a discussion on the topic, and Mr. Izetbegovic is actually taking part in that discussion. So according to you, Witness, did Izetbegovic recognise the HVO as a constituent part of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or did he not recognise that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He recognises the HVO as a constituent part of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; no doubt about that. Nevertheless, he appointed Delic a member of the BH Presidency, which could only happen in a duality with Petkovic, and that is the whole point. The entire transcript -- or, rather, a portion of the transcript is exactly about that. The HVO is on an equal footing with the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Registrar, could we have page 2 of this document on the screen, as well as the corresponding page in B/C/S. Witness, take a look at Boras's intervention with the president, Izetbegovic, taking the floor right after him. This is what Izetbegovic says, and I quote: "We can put the question of the status of the armed forces on the agenda in the future, how to resolve the issue. We tried -- if you remember, we wanted to resolve the matter with joint commands." So military-wise, what did Izetbegovic mean, according to you? He is actually taking the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, he was trying to say that the joint command did not succeed, although attempts were being made. At the time, had it not -- at the time, the joint command was not there, at least not the way he imagined it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question, and then I will hand the floor back to Mr. Scott. He has 50 minutes left. Very early on in this hearing, at 2.20, I think, Mr. Scott started with the first document, the first document he showed you. We don't have to look at it again, but it was a document signed by Mate Boban. In this document, signed by Mate Boban, P155, on April 10, 1992, April 10, Mr. Boban says that the TO, which is a service of the Serbo-Chetnik armada, does not exist for Croats in Herceg-Bosna, and he requests for military units of the HVO to be created. When you were in the field, and then after that all questions put to you by Mr. Scott were quite relevant, and I would have put exactly the same ones as he did, but there's one thing I would like to know. I would like to know whether on April 10, 1992, the Territorial Defence existed in Herceg-Bosna, manned by Muslims, including Muslims, or was there none, and because there was none, Mate Boban took advantage of that void to say where there's nothing exists, the Croats will set up these units? According to your recollection, can you tell us whether there were units of the Territorial Defence with a Muslim component? Let me give you an example. Kiseljak, for example, we saw a document shown to you by the Prosecutor where Blaskic is organising, so I would like to know whether in Kiseljak there were Muslim units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the time that we are talking about there was no Territorial Defence. As such, it existed back in Yugoslavia. At the time, the Territorial Defence had no weapons, was not properly organised. It had fallen apart. The Serbs had left. There are only files in certain municipalities; in other words, Territorial Defence documents. The Territorial Defence was now to be built back up, an army, forces to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina. The name, itself, the TO, was no more but a name. In Kiseljak, there was the HVO and an incipient TO or, rather, the BH Army. When I arrived in Central Bosnia, I found a lot of armed individuals, 90 per cent of them Croats. The Muslims had no weapons and were not organised, in the sense of being able to put up resistance. It wasn't before the second half of May or June that they were able to perform any military activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott asked you a question, and I would have asked the same one. He asked you what you did, yourself, to come into contact with the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the armed forces of the Presidency. And you answered by saying you did nothing. But there was one additional question that he forgot to put to you, and I will put it to you. What did the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina do in order to come into contact with you? Obviously, nothing was done between you and Sarajevo, in that direction, but did something come from the other direction? Because at one point in time you said, I met Mr. Boras, the same "Boras" that we see quoted in this document which is on the screen, so could you tell us what Sarajevo actually did in your direction? And if it's Mr. Boras who actually contacted you, could you tell us what he told you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Colonel Suvalic arrived in Vitez. He was the head of the Territorial Defence of the Zenica District already in Yugoslavia, and he said, "We're creating an army, be the head of staff and we've resolved the whole issue." So Colonel Suvalic has various files in the JNA garrison with the tanks and so on and so forth, he still had all that. I had already resolved the question of the garrison in Travnik, in the sense of me being a hostage. But he went out, he was creating an army, he had some soldiers and some units, and so I said, Well, establish an army and we'll go into battle together. He couldn't still go into battle because he didn't have the wherewithal, so I said, Set up your units and we can go into battle. And it would have been easier for me, I said, to be Chief of Staff, but that's not going to get us anywhere. So that was the relationship we had with the Territorial Defence, but not Sarajevo. He didn't have any connection with Sarajevo, either, when he was with me, at least not the kind of connection and contacts for battle and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Mr. Boras, what did he tell you? You told Mr. Scott that you saw Boras. What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think Boras was there during those days. There were a lot of events going on, but the basic thing is that Boras said that in Sarajevo, things were becoming a little more organised, and that when I informed him about what I was doing, a defence line had to be set up, first and foremost, so that the Army of Republika Srpska could not take control of any area that was not defended, that was the basic thing, Jajce, Bugojno, Travnik and so on, and he said, Carry on what you're doing, you're doing good. So there was nothing about subordination, re-subordination, or things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are telling us that Mr. Boras was a member of the Presidency and said, Go on, it's very good that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, your own testimony has contradicted you, which is one of the reasons I spent so much time on some of your testimony last week. You said, under oath, just a matter of a couple of days ago, that when you arrived in Central Bosnia things were disorganised, there were few armed individuals, you had to establish the HVO, essentially, from scratch. You also said that within a very short time, the Territorial Defence was, in fact, larger, more powerful, and had more professional officers than the HVO, by May or June. And you gave us the example, in fact, by May, of 2.000 Muslim soldiers arriving in Central Bosnia and becoming to you what you considered to be some sort of threat, in May 1992. There was a TO, sir --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object. This is a completely erroneous presentation of General Filipovic's testimony about the moment he arrived in Central Bosnia, which was the 10th of April, that general period, until June. This is a completely wrong interpretation of what he said. Now, if Mr. Scott considers that he is conveying the witness's testimony properly, then let him tell us the pages of the transcript where he said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have absolutely no doubt that's exactly what the witness said. And if he doesn't remember that, then I'll leave it to the Chamber to review the testimony. It's exactly what he talked about, and he said --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm not going to have counsel dictate my examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really do consider that we should respect the Rules applied in this Tribunal during the cross-examination, and could you please tell Mr. Scott that if he is referring to the testimony of this witness, or is he referring to any portion of the examination-in-chief or cross-examination by the Defence counsel, that he could tell us what the pages of the transcript are, because it is our right to check and see if the Prosecutor is correctly interpreting the testimony of this witness or not. And the fact that he is completely convinced that his interpretation is the correct one, I have no doubt that even if Mr. Scott is wrong on certain points, that he is wrong in good faith, but it is my task to point this out. And I'm sure that Mr. Scott has noted down all the relevant pages of the transcript, so can he just inform us what those pages are where the witness said what he's saying he said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're both right. Mr. Scott does not have the exact transcript pages, so he can't give you the right page number. He is right in saying that the Judges are going to check. Of course they will. And you're right, too, because it would be better to make sure there is no mistake, and if Mr. Scott refers to the witness's testimony, he has to be precise. But we have the witness here, we're lucky in that, so he can either say that Mr. Scott is right or tell Mr. Scott that he's wrong. The only one who is able to settle the matter without the transcript pages being shown is the witness. Did you follow what has just been said, because Mr. Scott says one thing, Ms. Alaburic says that she wants to have the right page number? From memory, do you remember what you testified earlier, or, I mean, if it goes back nine years, do you still remember what you said then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not only nine years ago, but three days ago. The Prosecutor is saying that I am not telling the truth, that I'm not answering his questions, that I'm not being precise enough, and so on and so forth. And as for the last question that he put to me, it is one thing to talk about the 10th of April, and it's another thing to talk about the 10th of April and my arrival in the area, because I said exactly what I found. I said I came across many armed individuals, but that wasn't an army, it wasn't an organisation being put in place. And already at the end of May and the beginning of June, and I said that as well, the Territorial Defence, with the arrival of cadres from the JNA --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rest assured, I didn't fall; just my binder did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I even named names, when it came to June 1992, from Lendo, Alagic, Cuskic, and all the others, not to have to enumerate them now. The BH Army -- the Territorial Defence of BH Army was stronger in terms of numbers than the HVO; in professional cadres, in the number of troops, armed combatants, and so on, and it was increasing in strength. And that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Which is exactly what I represented, and accurately so. And for one example, now that we've had the time, I refer the courtroom and Ms. Alaburic to page 47652 of last week's transcript, where the witness testified in April, May, June 1992, and in a very short time -- and by May or June of 1992, the Muslim armed forces were larger and had a larger professional officer corps. And I'm sure that can be further checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Further, in reference to questions put by Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me just say, then, what the witness said applying to June 1993, he said was happening in May -- I misspoke. I meant to say "1992," and once again it's being wrongly interpreted by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to continue this process of going back and forth and back and forth on what's being said or not said and what I said. The transcript is very clear. I just gave one example of the witness's prior testimony, when he was talking about April, May, June of 1992, and it's exactly as I represented it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Another question put to you, sir, by President Antonetti, in terms of communications and the existence -- the existence of the TO, the new TO, and communications from it, would you please turn to 1D00970, 1D00970. If I can have the usher's assistance, please, so we can move as quickly as possible. Perhaps we can have it on the -- we do have it on the screen. If we can just proceed that way, Your Honours. Both the English and the Croatian version is on the screen. Sir, if you can look on your screen, please? If you can look on the screen, please, sir, this is the communication from the Jablanica Municipal Assembly dated the 6th of May, 1992. The beginning part: "At its meeting held on 6 May 1992, the Jablanica Crisis Staff decided to organise a unified defence system for the Jablanica municipality area and hereby issued the following: "Announcement. All citizens of the Jablanica municipality are hereby notified that a unified defence system is being organised in our municipality and will consist of the Territorial Defence forces, the Croatian Defence Council, the Green Berets, and all others who wish to place themselves under the unified command of the Territorial Defence headquarters in Jablanica." Now, can you tell us, sir, after the 6th of May, 1992, what steps did the HVO take to place itself under the unified command of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. We're dealing with Jablanica municipality. Now, from the testimony, the witness at that time was in Central Bosnia the whole time, so how can the witness say what the HVO did in Jablanica or did not do?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, how can he say what happened in a meeting that he wasn't in attendance at?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I might -- this is one example -- this is one example, and I go back to -- the question came up, What communications from the TO? You said a few moments ago the TO didn't exist in Herzegovina. You said so under oath. Now, here's a document from the 6th of May, 1992, talking about the Territorial Defence and trying to organise a unified defence under a unified command structure, which you said the TO didn't exist in Herzegovina. And I put this to you as one example, but I come back to the question I put to you 45 minutes ago: What steps did the HVO take to put itself under the unified command of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I never said that the TO did not exist in Jablanica, which the Prosecutor has just said. I was just saying that in the first days of my arrival in Central Bosnia, the HVO was stronger in the sense of preparedness on the part of the population for defending themselves against an aggression, because they'd already experienced Vukovar, Ravno, et cetera. And the Muslims, thanks, among other things, to the statement made by Alija Izetbegovic, when he said, It's not our war, they were not prepared. So April and the first half of May was the -- during that time, the only real force in the area of Central Bosnia was the HVO. The Territorial Defence was being established. It was looking for commanders, it found some commanders, and sometime in June 1962 [as interpreted] was on an equal footing and stronger than the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to turn to a different topic because the record on this will quite clearly speak for itself, a question from last week. Let me ask you that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Witness, just in the wake of the Prosecutor's questions and following this document of the presidential transcript of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, isn't this the evidence that the municipalities were required to set up a military system, gathering all those on location? In Jablanica, it was the Green Berets and the Croats from the HVO, but there could have been other types of systems? And the interesting thing about this document is that the president of the municipality says that this does not preempt on other political solutions that may crop up later on, so does this mean that back in May 1992 -- so from memory I believe that by then the VRS was being set up in the Republika Srpska. There were in some municipalities some military formations -- joint military formations being created, as shown by this document shown by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, paper soldiers and papers, there was a lot of that, and I see here at this Tribunal now that there was a lot of that. Roso, Blaskic, the president of the municipality. Papers were flying hither and thither. The problem was, on the ground, to establish a defence. Now, in the document that's just been quoted, the Jablanica document, it says that the Green Berets ought to be unified, which means that they weren't in the Territorial Defence up until that time, and that the Patriotic League should be united and unified, and the HVO, too. So that's what was said here. It says here what should be done with the aim of realising an ideal situation, which this president says, whether he received a piece of paper, a document to that effect, or whether he wrote it himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to another topic, sir, and this is in connection with the time that you've told us when you and Mr. Pasalic were -- stayed for a time at the Spanish Battalion base near Dracevo. And I put it to you, sir, that last week you went -- again, went out of your way to create a false impression for these Judges, didn't you? And I'll tell you why so you don't have to guess. You knew full well, didn't you, that the reason that Pasalic was held and the reason that you couldn't enter Mostar at the time was because the HVO wouldn't let Pasalic go anywhere else or enter Mostar, and you knew that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection to the question. What is has the HVO got to do with Pasalic, when we had several witnesses before this Trial Chamber testifying about the fact that Pasalic was in an UNPROFOR vehicle, and how could the HVO do anything with respect to people who were under UNPROFOR's protection? So I'd like Mr. Scott to be more precise and say what he means exactly, because he was thinking about the 8th to the 9th of May, 1993, then he has no grounds, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, that's something that's just not true. And the witness said last week, and this -- I do have it from the 1st of December, the daily transcript, pages 43 to 47 -- what this witness ultimately said was, in answer to this question: "So can you now, General, comment on this assertion made; was that the truth or not about Mr. Pasalic being held by the HVO?" And Mr. Filipovic gave this answer under oath last week: "The route we followed passes mostly through an area controlled by the BH Army, and I don't know how the HVO could prevent Arif Pasalic from leaving the APC." And I put it to you, sir, that you did know exactly how because you knew -- let me conduct my examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really have an objection now. I think that I have been very patient in listening to Mr. Scott, to see the way in which he is conducting his cross-examination, and I hope that in redirect I'll try to illustrate facts to the Trial Chamber, but this is a completely wrong interpretation of the whole part of that testimony and examination of the witness. It was very clear that the question related to the case -- the Prosecution case that Arif Pasalic, on the 9th of May, 1993, was not in Mostar, because the HVO would have prevented him from entering Mostar. That was the Prosecution case. Now, we proved -- we showed that at the time he was in an UNPROFOR vehicle. And if my colleague, Mr. Scott, now wants to make any statements in that regard, let him present the question and answer in its entirety, not to go halfway, because otherwise it would be a completely erroneous depiction of what was happening in the courtroom. So Arif Pasalic was in an UNPROFOR vehicle. He was going from Jablanica to Dracevo. He was passing through East Mostar. And had he wanted to leave the vehicle, he could have done that. And that's the crux of the matter. The HVO couldn't control that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you turn, please, to P11138. And I'm going to ask the usher assist us, please, and to please stand by the witness so we can move as quickly as possible. My time is really very limited. P11138. This is a Spanish Battalion report. I refer you to -- it's in the next binder. Sorry, it's in the loose -- no, this one. Sorry, which one? My apologies. This is a separate document. I thought it had been distributed. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, while you're looking for that document and having it distributed, might I be allowed to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not going to have the witness talking on my time without answering my question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Witness. We're going to receive this document, just as you are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it's about the last question to which Ms. Alaburic objected, and I said nothing. So I assume I'm in this courtroom to say something, to be allowed to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Consider the question withdrawn until we have this document in front of us. There is no pending question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the question was withdrawn, but it may return with this document; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you'll please turn, in P1138, item 6.1 of this report -- item 6.1 "Other information": "At 1850, a Spanish convoy escorting Brigadier Pasalic and Colonel Filipovic was detained at control point E5. At 2008, an officer of the HVO military police presented himself at the above-mentioned control point, reinforcing it, and encouraging him men to adopt an aggressive attitude towards the Spanish convoy. Authorisation to continue was given at 2100, but at 2140 the convoy was again detained at the Vrapcici check-point, where allegations were made at the existence of uncontrolled groups that are mining the roads." Now, if you can turn to Exhibit P02241 in the same small binder, P02241. I'm going to move very quickly through these documents, usher. This is another Spanish Battalion report. Item 1.1, under "Areas of Responsibility," "Check-points": "On the 9th of May, 1993, after painstaking consultations with Mr. Bozic," I put it to the Chamber that is Slobodan Bozic, HVO, "the Spanish patrol providing escort protection for Brigadier Pasalic and Colonel Filipovic was allowed through the check-point at Vrapcici with the proviso that it must not enter Mostar and must make its way directly to Dracevo." Going to Exhibit P02235 in the same small binder, P02235 "Other Activities," page 5 of the English report: "Transport and escort protection were provided for general Pasalic and General Filipovic from Jablanica to Mostar. The HVO refused this escort entry after a wait of more than seven hours. The persons escorted were taken to Dracevo, where they spent the night and where they still remained." Please turn to Exhibit P1139, P1139, another Spanish Battalion report for the 10th and 11th of May. 5th item under "Mostar": "General Pasalic, commander of the 4th Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, continues to be at the Spanish Detachment in Dracevo. The HVO has set up check-points around the Spanish Detachment to prevent him from leaving ." That's why, sir, Mr. Pasalic -- where Mr. Pasalic was and why he couldn't move freely, and why he couldn't be in Mostar on the 8th, 9th, and 10th of May, 1993, and you conveniently forgot to tell that to the Chamber, but, in fact, created the impression with President Antonetti that it was the international forces who had arrested the two, and you knew full well that you were creating a false impression with these Judges when it was the HVO that controlled where Mr. Pasalic was; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, everything that I've said is correct, and I'll state it again. At a meeting in Konjic and Jablanica, we were there, Pasalic and I, but I had a higher function than he did. I occupied a higher post in the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the time, I was a member of the Joint Command, the number 2 man of this one side or the fourth man or third man within the entire overall Joint Command, whereas Pasalic was commander of a corps. Now, if the HVO prevented Filipovic's entry -- or, rather, Pasalic's entry, and if they prevented Pasalic from entering, they prevented Filipovic, too, that would be nonsense. That's one point. Secondly, before the convoy set out from Jablanica, the HVO could not influence its departure. For four or five hours, the convoy was unable to depart because Mr. Pasalic did not want the convoy to set out for some reason of his own, and he kept arguing with Major Carlos. I assume the man's still alive, so he'll be able to tell you. Now, as to the check-points that we were talking about, I know nothing about them because I was shut up in an APC together with Pasalic. He couldn't see anything; I couldn't see anything. And I woke up in Dracevo. It was 3.00 or 4.00 a.m., and Pasalic woke up then, too, because -- well, now you're implying that I knew that it was -- that Pasalic was not allowed to step down from the APC and some other things. We were arrested by the Spanish Battalion, with all four sides of the container being guarded. There were guards at all four points, so neither he nor I could leave and go anywhere. I said that, I'm saying that again, and I can confirm it 100 more times if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you were a senior commander in the HVO, you were in these vehicles. You were held at HVO check-points for at least seven hours on one occasion. And you're telling us that during that time, as a senior commander of the HVO, you never communicated to the HVO soldiers at the check-point, being held seven hours? You never looked outside, never asked a question?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we were both shut up in that APC. We would stop and then go, and then stop and then go again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to another topic, sir, unless the Judges have questions on that item. I'm going to move forward. Or the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before the break, Witness: There are two versions of what happened, yours, and you're under oath, and the Prosecutor's. He is contesting or challenging your version, using the Spanish documents, which are very clear and which state that there were these check-points and that Mr. Pasalic could not go where he wanted to go because he was prevented by the HVO, which was blocking traffic. Now, of course, your version is different. You maintained your version when you answered Mr. Scott. I was quite surprised, and I put that question to you. I asked you why it was that you couldn't contact the HVO, and you told me, No, we were prisoner. Even though we wanted to go to the bathroom, you know, we were escorted. So listening to Mr. Scott and listening to you, well, we have two different versions. Either you're not telling the truth or the Spaniards, to make sure that they could have you at hand. Both of you mentioned check-points and also mentioned rogue groups -- they're blaming this on the HVO, of course, but they are calling them rogue groups, rather than anything else. In this document, you know, I always look at the original version when I have a document, and in the Spanish document, in Spanish, document P11138, we have the Spanish stamp and on this because the Spaniards have this habit of putting stamps everywhere. Well, this document was written on May 8 at 11.30 p.m., and you know that events occurred on the next day, on May 9th in Mostar. Now, in this Spanish document, it says that someone from the HVO informed them of the possibility of a confrontation during the night between the ABiH and the HVO. This is what is written in this document. So are you 100 per cent sure Mr. Pasalic and yourself were kept by the Spaniards, detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as I said, there was a discussion between Pasalic and Carlos in Jablanica for several hours in order for the convoy to start out. Throughout that journey, both on the French side and on the American side, whenever we got into an APC we were unable to communicate with anyone. Therefore, for the duration of that journey, neither Pasalic nor I were in a position to communicate with anyone. We did not know what was going on outside; neither of us did. When we woke up, when the Spaniards opened the door of the APC, we were there among containers in Dracevo. All they asked us was whether we would go on being together in that container. We said, No problem. And we were placed in a container under the strictest -- closest possible monitoring. I don't think even the Spandau prison was anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. If I may, could you ask the witness a technical question? Why does SpaBat not describe, in its reports, that it drove at least seven kilometres through Mostar, which was under the control of the BH Army, and why did Pasalic not bang on the wall of the APC for the head of the convoy to stop? Why do the Spaniards never say that they drove for seven kilometres through East Mostar, that was under the control of the BH Army and no one else? We saw that a hundred times, Your Honours. Why, then, does Pasalic not bang against the wall of the APC for them to stop, because he could have done whatever he liked? Dracevo is a mere 15 kilometres south of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, unfortunately we do not have a map at hand, because with a map we could have followed the convoy to see exactly where it passed. But General Petkovic is saying that according to him - of course, it's his version and might not be yours - that you went through -- you must have gone through part of a road that was under the control of the Muslims. Is that possible or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possible territory under the control of the BH Army on that route. It's too big to be ignored. No reason to believe that the area through which we travelled was not under the control of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were in that APC, couldn't you see the outside; yes or no? Are you like in a tin can?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. There's an opening through which a Spanish soldier was looking. We could look through the opening, too, but all we saw was the sky, but not in terms of our putting our eye right against the opening; rather, right beside the opening. Therefore, the view from that opening, as far as we in the APC were concerned, was zero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this APC was stopped at check-points, since there was an opening, you must have heard voices asking -- you know, people from the UNPROFOR asking -- people asking the UNPROFOR where they were going when you were arrested. Didn't you hear voices, conversations, did you overhear them at least?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The APC was stationary for hours. When I say "for hours," it was stopped wherever it was stopped. We were only able to see part of the surrounding terrain and part of the sky. The talks, negotiations, were there any, we weren't able to tell. It was impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But couldn't you overhear anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we heard nothing. The engine was always on. The APC's engine was on constantly. Besides, I wasn't interested. In order for me to catch a glimpse of the surrounding terrain and know where I was, that would have been impossible. I couldn't have known. If Arif Pasalic could have looked outside through the opening and recognised the terrain, I certainly wasn't able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's five to 4.00. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Encouraged by Your Honour's comment about me being a stickler for precision the other day, just in case it misleads, I note in the English translation of 11138 there's a reference to the CIA. The CIA, we know they're everywhere, but they weren't here. I think it says "HVO sources have informed the CIA serving in the city." Your Honour, that appears to be -- Your Honour is in a position to confirm this. This comes from the Spanish, which is -- it's -- CIA is as an abbreviation, I think, there for "Al Compania," so I just wanted to note that in case anybody gets mislead by a rather strange reference to CIA in this English version of the document, it's nothing to do with the CIA as we know and love them at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right, Mr. Stewart. I hadn't noted that in the English version there is "CIA ," but in the Spanish version it says "Al Cap." So I thought it was the captain of the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I think the "CIA" is a Spanish abbreviation for "Al Compania." I think Your Honour would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Very well, I think everything is crystal clear now, and we'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, I'd like to turn to the topic of Sovici/Doljani, about which you were asked a number of questions. I'd like you to turn, first of all, please, to Exhibit P01933. It should be in the main binder, in numerical order, P01933. Sir, this is a report from Colonel Siljeg on the 17th of April, 1993. Just two quick questions.
