And the first item says that: "Due to T-130 actions ..." Can you just tell us, for the record, what's the "T-130" refer to?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Perhaps it's a type of cannon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And several items below that, if you'll see the sentence: "BH Army forces in Sovici village are crushed, some soldiers and civilians are fleeing from Sovici and some are surrendering." Now, you have no reason to disagree with Mr. Siljeg that that was the state of affairs in Sovici on the 17th of April, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say, Yes, and I can't say, No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You have no reason to disagree with them? You have no basis to disagree with Mr. Siljeg; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The meeting that we saw the video of on the 4th of May, can you recall approximately the time of day? I know it was some time ago, but as approximately the best you can, when that meeting started and approximately when the meeting ended?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume that it started sometime at 9.30 or 10.00, and that it ended at about 12.00, 12.30. After that, we were supposed to go to -- to leave and go three different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And just so the record is very clear, when you say 9.30 to 10.00, you're talking about 9.30 to 10.00 in the morning until approximately 12.00 or 12.30 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, according to the transcript -- we weren't getting a translation of the meeting when we were actually seeing the video, but there was a transcript that went with it, and during that meeting Mr. Halilovic offers the -- "the hand of friendship" to the HVO, but raises a number of issues: the holding of Muslim men, expelled Muslims from their homes, Mostar becoming a detention centre. And he wanted questions from Mr. Petkovic on those points; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true, what Sefer was saying, and it's true, also, what Petkovic was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And wouldn't you agree with me, sir, that based upon the grievances that Mr. Halilovic and Mr. Pasalic were expressing on that day, they had some reason to be upset, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the meeting at Jablanica occurred 10 days after an intense round of meetings in Central Bosnia, where we also held meetings --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, our time is limited. Mr. Pasalic and Mr. Halilovic had reasons to be upset, didn't they; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I won't testify here by saying yes or no. I didn't spend all the time and all the energy to do that. I'm telling you what was going on. At that meeting, for me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- what Sefer said was actually shocking, and also what Arif Pasalic said was also shocking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are here to answer the questions put to you by the Prosecutor. In this procedure, the Prosecutor is allowed to give his point of view, saying that this meeting didn't unfold correctly, yes or no. It's his point of view. Just answer, Yes, or No. And then if he wants to know why you don't agree with him, he will ask you why and press on. He is conducting his cross-examination the way he wishes. I'm sure that Ms. Alaburic told you about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, he asked me -- he put it to me that Arif Pasalic and Sefer Halilovic had reason to act the way they did. I don't know if they had reason or not. I'm just trying to say what I found shocking. I found shocking what they actually said and how they said it at the meeting, which was very different from anything they previously said at any of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You don't know? You the answer is you don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, one of the things that came up at that meeting was that Mr. Pasalic complained about the HVO's arrest of 14 of his soldiers, that is, Mr. Pasalic's soldiers, the night before. And when the issue was raised with Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Petkovic says, and this is at page 11 of the transcript: "Give me a list of the 14 people arrested, and they will be freed tonight, after I get back to Mostar." You were then asked by Ms. Alaburic, after the video was played: "Now, did General Petkovic demonstrate readiness for co-operation? What was your impression about his real intentions and wishes? "A. Our side, on the whole, as a whole, wanted, wished, and endeavoured to do that." So on the one hand, sir, you have this representation by Mr. Petkovic that he's about to see to the immediate release of 14 men held captive by the HVO, but I'd like you to look, please, next at Exhibit P02182, P02182. While you're doing that, sir, to use the time, this is an order from Mr. Petkovic to Stipe Polo or Pole on the 4th of May, 1993, at 2200 hours, we can see at the top part of the page. Now, sir, this is the same Stipe Polo or Pole who you've told -- you've mentioned several times as one of your sources of information as to what happened in Sovici/Doljani; correct? Correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. Petkovic gives this order to Mr. Pole: "Release all detained civilians in Doljani and Sovici, keep men fit for military service." Now, I'm going to take those in reverse order. When you were collecting information that you told us about last week, in talking to Mr. Polo, in talking to some of the others that you said you talked to, did you obtain this information that it was Mr. Petkovic who had ordered that all the Muslim men be detained?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know, to your knowledge, whether there was any effort to distinguish or classify the Muslim men, those who had actually been engaged in combat and those who had not been?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any cases where a distinction was drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, this is the 4th of May, 1993. I want to take us back to one of our earlier topics today. This is after the cease-fire dated the 20th of April, 1993. This is after the joint statement by Boban and Izetbegovic on the 25th of April, 1993, in which everything was supposed to be at peace and the armies were supposed to join together and fight together. In that circumstance, why would Mr. Petkovic order the detention of the Muslim men? Peace had broken out. You were on the same side, according to you. Why hold the Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Scott. I might be lost somehow. I have here a paper where Mr. Petkovic orders the release. I have not seen any order that they be detained. Maybe I missed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps at the end of the sentence, sir, after "Sovici," you'll see: "... keep men fit for military service." Does that assist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's what I [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay, it's not "arrest," it's "continued detention" that is ordered, so in this way it's slightly equivocal. But thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why keep holding Muslim men, sir, at this time?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to ask Mr. Scott to be as precise as possible. Here, we are clearly talking about able-bodied men of military age, and not just generic Muslims. Therefore, I think there's a need to be as specific as possible here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There's no need for that intervention. The document says plainly what it says, "keep men fit for military service," and doesn't change my question at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There's a cease-fire, there's an agreement, you're saying the HVO is a legitimate part of the BiH armed forces, We're on the same side. Why hold -- continue to hold the Muslim men of any description, as ordered by General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered that already. I said I don't know about them being detained. I don't know if the document is authentic. I don't know why men fit for military service were separated off.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know why this -- going to the first part, "Release all detained civilians in Doljani and Sovici...," do you know why the civilians had been detained?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I've said already, I know nothing about Sovici and Doljani, apart from the talks I had at the base in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, that's exactly my point, and that was the point of my objection during your direct examination. You're giving testimony about something you knew nothing about. You simply don't know what happened at Sovici/Doljani; correct? You can't have --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, there's no need for an intervention here. The witness can't have it both ways. He can't say, I'm going to testify about Sovici/Doljani or I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, I don't know why Mr. Scott appears to be losing his temper in the course of this examination. The witness clearly said he knew nothing about the events at Sovici and Doljani, but he said he knew about the agreement -- about the evacuation of people from Sovici and Doljani. He knew about them leaving for Gornji Vakuf and from then on to Jablanica. But that's a different subject altogether. That doesn't mean the witness knows what was going on in Sovici and Doljani, who was detained where, and how many people were detained. The witness clearly said very clearly what he knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, let General Filipovic answer. He's able enough to understand a question and to answer questions. It's a waste of time if you have irrelevant objections. The Prosecutor asked the witness why civilians were detained, as stated in the document. Well, the witness can say, I wasn't there, I don't know anything about it, and then a question can be asked whether it was normal to detain civilians. And he might answer then, Yes, No. Please continue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A reference that was just made to an evacuation. That's part of the point. You don't know what the conditions were, you don't what happened in Sovici/Doljani, you don't know in what conditions the Muslim women and children were being held, or what had happened to them, or what had happened to the men, do you? So when you say "evacuation," that's your characterisation of something that you don't know anything about; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know about Sovici and Doljani is what I talked about with Biskit [phoen], Ola, Zuka, and Nihad.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, that this Tribunal has specifically rejected the characterisation of this as an evacuation?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let's just try to be specific. Which Chamber? In Croatian, the interpretation we got was "this Chamber," this Chamber dismissed something or has rejected a characterisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This Tribunal, this Tribunal in the Tuta Stela case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that means some other Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know how -- you said that you were involved in arranging the buses that did come. How did you -- what arrangements did you make to have the buses arrive in Sovici? Who did you contact, what arrangements did you put in place?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I checked to see whether the buses had been sent to Sovici and Doljani.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about you checked to see if they had. What arrangements did you make? Who did you contact in order to arrange for the buses to be sent? Did you talk to -- you talked to Slobodan Bozic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to someone in the Main Staff. I think it was the duty officer or someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where did the buses come from?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have been listening very carefully to your answer. It is a relevant answer, but in another respect regarding Mostar. The Prosecutor asked you how you organised yourself to send buses, and you said that you called somebody at the Main Staff. In other words, whenever there was this kind of logistical problem when you had to dispatch buses and drivers, the buses must have fuel, they must have a destination. So in your view, it was the Main Staff that organised all that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because Petkovic told them, Check to see if the buses had been sent to Sovici and Doljani. I don't know where from -- or, rather, at that point in time I couldn't have known from where the buses had been sent, who had organised it. But it turns out that it was organised by the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So did General Petkovic ask you to check whether the buses had been sent? He didn't ask you to organise the dispatching; he just asked you to check, didn't he? In other words, somebody else organised the question of the buses. You just checked, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us imagine that you encountered a problem regarding the transportation of civilians at your level, so some civilians have to be evacuated. Who do you have to turn to to have them be evacuated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably the civilian authorities, because the Main Staff, I don't know whether it had any buses. So the civilian authorities were the ones who were supposed to organise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But then in this instance of Sovici and Doljani, why is it that it was taken care of by the Main Staff and not by civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because Sefer, the way you saw him on the video, and Petkovic talked, discussed, agreed, and I don't know why the Main Staff dealt with that, or, rather, Petkovic. Probably at the request of Sefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yet, you know, my questions are extremely important, as you can imagine. I just don't ask a question for the sake of it. I don't waste my time asking useless questions. Whenever civilians are evacuated, there may arise problems because of the state of their health, the food, et cetera. In such an environment, shouldn't it be the Civilian Protection that should take care of all this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly it should have, it should have been dealt with by the Civilian Protection. But for everything to be successful, the HVO had to involve itself to see that everything went without a hitch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let me return to Sovici/Doljani. And imagine that General Petkovic hears that following fighting, there are civilians to be evacuated because there are problems; either to protect them or for any other reason. Shouldn't he have turned to the Civilian Protection to take over the problem? Why did he take care of the problem in person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know whether it was him or not. He told me to check and see if the buses had left or gone to Sovici and Doljani. That's what I know. Now, who organised it, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the thing to be remembered is that you just checked, and the rest escapes you. Fine. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Turning to a moment on another topic. On military discipline, sir, you said in your Kordic testimony that HVO commanders had authority to take disciplinary measures against their subordinates at various levels; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had authority on paper, according to the rules or whatever they were, but in actual fact they could do very little, except if there was a large mistake made, then there was the prison in Busovaca where they were sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Those in the military chain of command were involved in military disciplinary investigations, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you said -- one of the things you said in your previous testimony -- excuse me, my apologies. One of the things that Mr. Petkovic said in his testimony in the Blaskic case, that one of the things a commander can do is to detain a subordinate for up to 15 days of detention. Correct? You would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree with that. I mean, it's correct, except for the question of where they would be detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Petkovic also testified in the Blaskic case that Colonel Blaskic had the authority to punish any officers or soldiers -- HVO soldiers who were involved in the crimes or misconduct at Ahmici. Would you agree with Mr. Petkovic that Blaskic had that authority?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crime in Ahmici surpassed the incarceration of soldiers, it went beyond that. The crime in Ahmici took place after combat, but the crime -- and nobody is denying it, but the crime surpassed this 15-day incarceration period or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. My specific question was -- and this is in Mr. Petkovic's Blaskic testimony at page 24166: "Blaskic had the authority to punish any HVO officers or soldiers who were involved in the crimes or misconduct at Ahmici." Now, do you agree or disagree with Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blaskic had the authority to detain an officer or a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You just mentioned, in response to the question that I put to you about Ahmici, that Blaskic had this authority. In fact, sir, you testified previously at this Tribunal in the Kordic case that you really were fairly dismissive of the crime at Ahmici, weren't you? You said that the -- what happened at Ahmici and the issues there was not something very important until some years later, when you said this impression that was created was "orchestrated or fabricated." That's the testimony you gave in the Kordic case, isn't is it?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that for the first few days after Ahmici -- or Santici, rather, it wasn't -- well, at all the meetings from the 20th onwards, the question of Ahmici wasn't raised, or Santici, in that sense, and not several years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is the testimony you gave at page 17054 to 55 in the Kordic case about Ahmici: It was not something special until later, 1994-1995, and it looked to you like it had been orchestrated like a "fabricated picture." That was the view you expressed of the controversy concerning Ahmici in your Kordic testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said then and I'm saying now, in those first days or in the first month, because I was constantly with the commanders from the BH Army, I've already said that I spent two nights in Konjic with them and two nights in Zenica, in the Joint Command, nobody raised this question of Ahmici or, rather, Santici. And so in that sense, it was only when Mazowiecki toured Ahmici that -- and in the world -- when the mosque was destroyed, that's when the real pressure began or, rather, the events in Ahmici became something a la Srebrenica, akin to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you testified in the Kordic case that it was not until 1994 or 1995 that the controversy about Ahmici was, in your words, orchestrated like a fabricated picture; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this picture about Ahmici had been raised, all my efforts -- everything positive that I had incorporated into the defence fell through because we were all criminals. That's how it was orchestrated then and now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're not answering my question, but I don't have time to pursue it further. In fact, sir, you didn't investigate any war crimes during the time you were in command, did you? You didn't direct that any be conducted, you weren't involved in any investigations of war crimes; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. [In English] I have objection. First, the witness should be asked whether he was -- whether he had any authority to perform investigation or criminal investigation, then if he -- depending on his answer, then he can be asked whether he did perform some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you didn't conduct any investigations of war crimes, didn't you? You testified in the Kordic case: "No, I didn't, I did not investigate war crimes." That's what you testified in the Kordic case; correct? Page 17239.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to join my colleague in objecting, and I'd like to ask my colleague, first of all, where it was prescribed that a military commander must instigate investigations to take proceedings. And if it is established that Mr. Filipovic occupied a post where that was possible, then he could be asked the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, for it to be clear for everybody: Earlier on, the Prosecutor told you that there had been no punishment. I sensed that there was going to be a problem, and I waited for the right time to ask my questions, and then there were objections by the Defence counsel. I'm taking not Ahmici, but a theoretical case. You command a unit, and a crime is committed. You are informed that a soldier, for instance, burned down a house or stole the money in the house and killed its inhabitants, and so you are being made aware of it. Tell me, if you go by the JNA rules at the time, what did it say and what did the HVO rules say? What is the military commander supposed to do? So this is a very clear question. What were you supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there's no dilemmas. Behind the JNA, you had the state, the system, and whatever else, but for the HVO in Central Bosnia, no courts functioned. You were not able to organise anything because everybody had an automatic rifle in their hands and all they had to do was to pull the trigger and 30 bullets would be shot. So I was required to say whether I conducted investigations or whatever, initiated them. First of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me stop you, General. My question was extremely specific. It couldn't be more specific, but I'll fine-tune it. You were in Travnik, and you learned that one of the soldiers burned down a house, stole the money out of the house, and killed the inhabitants of that house. What do you do? This is very clear. What are you going to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had to take steps to prevent anything like that from happening again. A soldier was incarcerated in a Travnik garrison for having killed an HVO member, and then the brother the next day of the victim killed this person who was in prison, so I'm trying to paint what the situation was like in reality. And for a commander to exercise his authority, you have to be backed up by a whole system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the example you gave of the brother, because that was a case you experienced yourself. But let's take another example. I'll go back to mine. A soldier burned down a house, stole money, and killed the inhabitants of the house. What steps do you have to take? What specific steps do you take immediately? What do you have to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should arrest the soldier and put him in prison, disarm him, and hand him over for an investigation. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, that was easy and specific. You have to arrest him, disarm him, and hand him over to the body in charge of investigations. Which are the bodies in charge of investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be the courts, the investigating judge, the whole system. But there was none of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So normally speaking, you should hand him over to the investigating judge and to the courts, but you say that all that did not exist. Did that not exist in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All over the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, you see, it's easy to answer specific questions. That's all I need, as far as I'm concerned. Please, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you next, please, to turn to Exhibit P11128, P11128. Can I have the usher's assistance, please. Can I have the usher's assistance, please. While the usher's assisting us, sir, and to use the time: By April of 1994, you were the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, or it might have been called at that point the Vitez Military District; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Vitez Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, that by April of 1994, Mr. Petkovic had once again become the head of the HVO military, had the number 1 position?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you became head of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, Colonel Blaskic had moved and taken a position in Herzegovina. Do you know what position Mr. Blaskic took at that time?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blaskic went to replace Petkovic, and I replaced Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So as of April 1994, is it correct, sir, that Mr. Petkovic was again the head of -- the number 1 person in the HVO military, Mr. Blaskic was number 2, and then you were head of the Military District in Central Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Blaskic took on those functions where it was Petkovic, when Blaskic took over them, Blaskic was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. Our time is too limited, unfortunately, to try to sort that out any further. If I can ask you to look at Exhibit P11128. This is a report by UNPROFOR. Let me just -- it's on page 3 of the English version, item 16, under "Sector South-West." The point is simply this, sir, if you can confirm for us, it says: "Commander, Vitez pocket, Filip Filipovic has been promoted from colonel to brigadier." Do you recall the approximate date on which you were promoted from colonel to brigadier?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in May 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you look, please, at P11129, P11129. Is it correct, sir, that around -- at the same time that you were promoted to brigadier, Mr. Ivica Rajic was promoted to the same rank, Mr. Kordic was promoted to the same rank, and Mr. Franjo Nakic was promoted to the same rank?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about Nakic for sure, I know as far as Kordic is concerned. Now, Ivo Lozancic and probably Ivica Rajic on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did it surprise you, sir, to see Mr. Kordic given the rank of brigadier, when you've said so many times that Kordic had no military role, no military involvement, was not a military commander?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A rank can be used for command, the command of units, but it can also be for other elements of organisation. For example, in 1992, Lucic in Kiseljak was given the rank of brigadier just because he had to negotiate in Kiseljak, so he had to have a rank, whereas he wasn't in command of anything, didn't command anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a moment. Could you ask what this person's first name was, Lucic? I think it was important, what this man Lucic was doing in Kiseljak. Could that question be asked, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, not on my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you surprised --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to my learned friend, but I don't have time, so that's why I intervened, although I know who it refers to. But I apologise for interfering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this Lucic person, Lucic person, could you give us his first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lucic. I can't remember his first name. I know him very well, and he was from Kiseljak. Lucic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's all you can say. In this document, we see that you signed after Mr. Ivica Rajic, who becomes brigadier, just like you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at that point in time it wasn't the rank of general. I became major general only in February 1995. So this was the rank of brigadier, the highest officer rank, but not the rank of general.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just tell you, Your Honours, that in the Croatian your question was mistranslated as if it was the rank of general that was being allotted. That's why you have the witness answering as he's just done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Brigadier was the second-highest rank in the HVO; there's only the rank of general higher than that?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did it surprise you, sir, to see Ivica Rajic being promoted to this very high HVO rank, in light of his history?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, he was the commander of the operative group, the tactical group, just like Ivo Lozancic in --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He was under your command, wasn't he, sir, when you became -- well, he was under your command both when you were the deputy commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone throughout most or at least the second half of 1993, and he was under your command when you became commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, correct, Mr. Rajic?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I became commander, Rajic was no longer in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, he was under your command, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was under my command while I was the deputy commander of the Military District, so in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, did you know -- throughout this period, did you know this man as Ivica Rajic or did you ever know him as Viktor Andric?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Washington Agreement and when I was able to go to Kiseljak, I saw that the commander of the brigade was Mijo -- Mijo --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You didn't answer my question. I don't know why, what the error might have been, but you didn't answer my question. This man that you say was promoted to brigadier on the same day that you were, Ivica Rajic, did you know him throughout that period as Ivica Rajic or did you ever know him as Viktor Andric?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him as Ivica Rajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You knew, a deputy commander, by the end of October of 1993, that there had been a huge alleged atrocity in Stupni Do and that Ivica Rajic was the principal suspect concerning that atrocity, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I learnt that after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's look at Exhibit P06182.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have five minutes left, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is an UNPROFOR press release, dated the 27th of October, reporting the Stupni Do atrocity. It also includes the fact that the UNPROFOR was kept out of Stupni Do by the HVO for three days before they could actually enter the village. Sir, this Chamber has heard extensive evidence about Stupni Do, the fact that it was reported literally around the world, in New York, at the UN, in the capitals of Europe, within a matter of days of it happening. This was in your area of command. You were the deputy commander. And I put it to you, sir, you could not possibly not have known about this huge controversy in your area of responsibility; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I'm claiming is that I didn't know and couldn't have known. Now, whether New York knew, I can't say. I know that as far as Ahmici is concerned, the whole world knew on the day when it happened. I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to Exhibit P07394, P07394. This is an order by General -- by Mr. Blaskic on the 30th of December, 1993, which he dismisses Ivica Rajic from his position. And the grounds given by Colonel Blaskic are: "Colonel Rajic is being dismissed from his duty due to a series of apparent weaknesses in command and control and an irresponsible influence on the units while carrying out combat operations." And I note that Mr. Blaskic's order is copied to the HVO Main Staff, to the HVO Ministry of Defence, et cetera. Now, with that document in mind, I ask you to turn next, please, to P09981, P09981. This is a document by the same Colonel Blaskic, dated the 5th of November, 1993, commending Mr. Rajic: "Your military attitude towards task and your huge contribution to the organisation of defence and salvation of Croats from Vares has been a great moral inspiration to all of us." So on the one hand, sir, we have Colonel Blaskic praising Ivica Rajic for a great organisation of military forces, for a terrific military attitude, for making a huge contribution, and for being a great moral inspiration to us all. Several weeks later, we have the same Colonel Blaskic dismissing the same man due to a series of apparent weaknesses in command and control and an irresponsible influence on the units. Now, sir, which one was it?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as to the time we're discussing, we had nothing to do with the Kiseljak enclave. It was 12 kilometres of territory that was controlled by the BH Army. Now, Blaskic, on two or three times, flew by helicopter from the Lasva Valley to the south, he flew south, and he could have learnt the truth or whatever else; I don't know. I could not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, please turn to -- and I'm closing, Mr. President. If you please turn to P07401, P07401. Sir, this is an order from the same Colonel Blaskic the very same day as one of the two that I showed you a moment ago, the 30th of December, 1993, appointing Colonel Viktor Andric to take command of the forward command post in Kiseljak. Sir, I put it to you that this -- all of this takes place right under your nose, as deputy commander of this operative zone, someone operating in the Vitez Hotel, as you told us the other day, only several metres from Mr. Blaskic's office, how documents and orders were prepared, and you could not have been a deputy commander of this operative zone and not known about this entire subterfuge. Viktor Andric and Ivica Rajic were one in the same person, weren't they, and you knew it?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, from the Command of the Military District, Krizancevo Selo is just a short distance away, 15 minutes away. Now, during these Christmas days of 1993, it was Christmas, there were many other things, and now I'm being shown a document and said that I must have known about it. I had nothing to do with all these papers. I wasn't a paper soldier. What I knew about were concrete things. So when I say I don't know, I'm not lying. I'm telling you what I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can be allowed one final exhibit, Mr. President, P07840, P07840.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I only have time to show you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last exhibit, please, because you're running out of time. You've run out of time, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I might finish this exhibit, Your Honour, and just two questions. P07840. I would be most appreciative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I only have time to show you one particular -- one of several illustrations, but this is a Security Council report dated the 10th of February, 1994, well before the awarding of Mr. Rajic to the brigadier rank that we saw a few moments ago. In paragraph number 12 of this Security Council report, in the second half of paragraph 12, Mr. Ivica Rajic is described as the main suspect. And I put it to you again, sir, this is was a matter of worldwide notoriety, it was the subject for the Security Council of the United Nations, and I put it to you, sir, that when you, on this same document, P11129, were promoted the very same day as Mr. Ivica Rajic, you knew exactly who Mr. Rajic was, you knew he had been called Viktor Andric, and you knew of his history, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't know. I had no way of knowing. I really don't know what Rajic was indicted for, was he in Stupni Do or not, or anything to do with that. Please take that into account. If I say I don't know, that means just that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor for your redirect.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think the best idea would be to have a break right now. I would like to organise my examination a little and start my redirect in what I believe will be the most efficient way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How long do you need for your redirect? You know that all the time you will use will be deducted from your overall time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my assessment now is that I can do whatever I think is necessary in about an hour. I hope that you, too, will be joining the discussion concerning some documents and some issues. That probably means that, in practical terms, we could keep on talking to this witness until the end of the day. And we might have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Had it been less, it would have been best to end the redirect with the witness and then to have the new witness after the break, but you're telling us that you need about an hour. Let me consult with my fellow Judges to see how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have a break, a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, just very quickly to mention that the Petkovic team and the Prosecution have agreed between ourselves, subject to Your Honours' approval, of course, that we might have until Thursday to file the IC lists of proposed exhibits following the end of this witness's evidence. So, Your Honours, would appreciate -- it sometimes is a bit tight for us, one witness coming after another. So if Your Honours are happy with that - I hope you are - that's what we've agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you agree, the matter is settled. Ms. Alaburic, the Trial Chamber would like to know which items you want to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thank you. Good evening to you. Good evening to my learned friends from the Prosecution, the witness, and everyone else. My subjects are as follows: Firstly, the arrival of Arif Pasalic in Dracevo, an analysis of documents shown by the OTP today and pointing on the map at all the locations that Arif Pasalic had to go through in order to reach Dracevo. The next subject is the JNA leaving all the barracks in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I will tell you, when the time comes, what that is in relation to. The third subject is about the video-clip and the speech given by Dario Kordic in Busovaca on the 16th of January, 1993. The fourth subject is General Filipovic's evidence in the Kordic case and the credence that the Chamber lent to its relevance in relation to Dario Kordic's command. The fifth subject is about the organigram of the HVO used by General Petkovic in the Blaskic case, who would have decided on the re-subordination of the Convicts Battalion. The sixth subject, on the status of men fit for military service. The seventh subject -- correction. The Kordic speech was given in 1992 and not in 1993, as I erroneously stated. I do apologise. The seventh subject is about the Prosecution and duties of a military commander in a situation when the perpetrator is unknown. The eighth subject would have to do with the legality and legitimacy of the HVO, very briefly. The ninth subject would be organising the HVO as a considerable military force in 1992 or later. And the 10th subject would be why was General Filipovic surprised by the fact that the indictments from this Tribunal raised against the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina started with Central Bosnia and not some other areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There will be a number of new documents being introduced. I think I will manage to ask my questions in an exceptionally brief way, and I hope that we'll be shedding new light on a number of matters. If I may, I would now like to move on to my first subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us analyse Arif Pasalic's departure for Dracevo in an UNPROFOR vehicle. General Filipovic, you drove in that UNPROFOR APC. Can you tell us what it looks --

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If there is someone inside, what about the person inside this vehicle; can this person decide when they'll stick their head out through the hatch, when he or she will leave the vehicle, or does the vehicle have to be opened by someone else?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I drove in an APC, the person who's being driven is entirely unable to affect anything at all, do anything at all, open the door of the hatch or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about the security aspect? Would it ever be allowed for someone who is inside an UNPROFOR vehicle, when the vehicle pulls over, to stick their head out to see where they were?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been impossible. There is a soldier who is inside the APC, and then there's a small opening, and through that opening you may be able to catch a glimpse of something or other.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, based on your information, if an UNPROFOR vehicle came to a check-point, would the UNPROFOR soldiers immediately tell the soldiers at the check-point who the persons were inside the vehicle, or was the information confidential?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was impermissible to ever give away such information at all as to who was inside the APC.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, when the convoy of APCs, carrying you and Arif Pasalic, came to any of the HVO check-points held by HVO soldiers, what about those HVO soldiers at the check-point; were they in a position to know who was inside which UNPROFOR vehicle?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We inside the vehicle didn't know who was outside. Those outside didn't know who was in the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Please, let me ask you again to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. We apologise if we were going too fast.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, you remember the SpaBat documents that we were looking at. There are two check-points specified there at which the UNPROFOR vehicles were stopped. The first is marked as "E-5," and the other was described as being near Vrapcici. Did you notice that as you were looking at those documents?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I know where Vrapcici is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we look at the SpaBat documents, it wasn't observed anywhere that after Vrapcici, the convoy was stopped at any other check-point before Dracevo, itself. I'm just stating the fact. I tried to look at the documents closely, and after Vrapcici there were no other check-points. Can we now please look at the map 4D1216. This is a map of the Mostar area. It's simple and somewhat stylised, but should be sufficient for our present purpose. General, I do have to admit I'm not sure if it's at the beginning or the end of your folder. It's a map in colour, red, blue and green. There it is. It's right there at the beginning. General, let's try to look at this map now. Can we please blow up the section around Mostar, itself. That's right, thank you. General, you can follow this on the screen in front of you. At the edge of the green area, around East Mostar, we can see "Vrapcici"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the north.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, if a vehicle reaches Vrapcici, it must be on M-17, the main road. If the vehicle is to head south, which route must it take?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has to drive down the left-hand riverbank of the Neretva River, east of Vrapcici, and then on towards Mostar, and then further south, about a kilometre further south, as far as trig point Hum 436, and then further east, about half a kilometre further east, and then south through Ortijes and then further south. We don't see Dracevo on the map, actually. Dracevo is at least 15 kilometres further south from Ortijes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's try to sum this up, General. A vehicle continues to move from Jablanica on to Vrapcici and then further south. This vehicle has to pass through East Mostar; right?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about East Mostar; is that the area marked in green here as being under the control of the Muslim authorities?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the entire area is like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The last SpaBat document that was shown is P11139, states HVO check-points were set up around Dracevo. To be quite specific, around Dracevo, to keep Arif Pasalic from leaving. General, given the fact that you spent four days in the area, during those four days did any UNPROFOR vehicles enter or, indeed, leave the Dracevo base?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We couldn't see that. But on the second or third day, a colonel of SpaBat was brought in who had been wounded in Sarajevo. Arif Pasalic and I could see the colonel and agreed immediately that he wouldn't make it. He had been wounded too badly, frankly, which means that there were vehicles going into the Dracevo base and leaving.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, under the assumption that the UNPROFOR vehicles were in a position to leave the Dracevo base, and that Arif Pasalic wanted to leave Dracevo in an UNPROFOR vehicle, could anyone have known that he was inside one of the UNPROFOR vehicles leaving Dracevo?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have got into an APC and nobody would have known about it, but he couldn't have asked to leave because for the first two days the Spaniards kept us in such a way that it was impossible to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly your evidence-in-chief, you and Arif Pasalic attended the Medjugorje meeting on the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Petkovic and Halilovic were there, too; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, at the time or at any time after, did Arif Pasalic tell you that he wanted to leave Dracevo but was unable to leave because of some HVO check-points around Dracevo?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no check -- or, rather, nothing was said about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arif Pasalic could not say anything about the check-points, firstly, because he couldn't see any and, secondly, because he had no reason to talk about that. He never mentioned any check-points.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that at the meeting in Medjugorje on the 12th of May there were also UNPROFOR representatives, for example, General Morillon and other representatives of the international community, at that meeting, or, indeed, at any time after, did anyone, to the best of your knowledge, ever say that the HVO had blocked the UNPROFOR base at Dracevo in order to keep Arif Pasalic from leaving?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one ever said that. Sefer, himself, didn't say that. Nothing was said about that at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next subject, General, the JNA leaving the Travnik compound. You were asked by Mr. Scott, at 476 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't hear the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: -- 47684, 684, and then the following three pages, this is roughly what Mr. Scott put to you: He first asked you when the JNA left the Travnik compound. You answered that this occurred on the 6th of May, 1992. Mr. Scott then went on to mention to you the meeting between Karadzic and Boban and the agreement they reached in Graz which occurred on the same day. He asked you whether the meeting at Graz, G-r-a-z, and the JNA leaving the Travnik compound were related in any way. Your answer was: "I don't think they were in any way related, but I can't rule out the possibility." Therefore, General, let me show you a number of documents now. The next document in your binder, the number is 4D2016, 4D2016, 4D2016 - that's right - this is an overview of the news published by the Croatian Information Centre. I'm only looking at two dates here, and that is the only translation into English that was done. General, please just listen to me. This is extremely brief. General, please pay attention to what I'm about to tell you. The 4th of May, 1992, the following piece of news: "The Presidency of Yugoslavia decided to withdraw the JNA from Bosnia within 15 days ..." The news in relation to the 15th of May, 1992, reads: "In Tuzla, Muslim extremists attacked the convoy of JNA soldiers withdrawing from Bosnia to Serbia. According to unofficial data, about 200 soldiers have been killed." And the next document, General, which is just in English, so listen to me - I'll read it out and ask you a question afterwards - it is 4D2017, that's the number of the next document, 4D2017 - yes, we have the right number now. Two sections relating to the JNA's withdrawal, chosen at random. The first has to do with Zejnil Delalic, the judgement, paragraph 116, and I'll read it out in English: [In English] "On 4th May 1992, the authorities in Belgrade announced that all JNA personnel who were not citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be withdrawn from the republic by 19 May. In consequence, approximately 14.000 JNA troops left Bosnia and Herzegovina." [Interpretation] Now I'm going to speak in B/C/S again for a while. The next topic was the Prosecutor versus Dusko Tadic, and this fact of the withdrawal of the JNA from the barracks in Bosnia and Herzegovina was the key date for deciding whether or not it was an international conflict or not. And in paragraph 571, opinion and judgement, the fact is presented, and I'm going to read out it in English again: [In English] "... after the withdrawal of the JNA on 19 May 1992." [Interpretation] That's the correct quotation. I have been told to put the date right on page 81, line 3, it should read "the 19th of May." Now, let me ask you this, General: If you remember, did the JNA withdraw just from Travnik or did it withdraw from all the areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina which were not under the control of the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the withdrawal from Travnik was the result of two or three days of negotiation with the commander. It had nothing to do with the 6th. That was done in the morning, but I had to negotiate with the commander for several days, and that's when an agreement was reached saying that every person leaving should just take their side-arms with them, and all the other details were agreed as well, and also that the most responsible people from Travnik, five on the Muslim side and five on the Croatian side, should be hostages for this column to be allowed to withdraw from one area to an area controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska. I was one of those hostages. Now, the question of whether all the -- whether from all the garrisons -- well, where the JNA was able to organise its withdrawal itself, it probably did so. It probably organised this in Tuzla. I don't know about Tuzla, but it wouldn't have left of its own accord from Travnik had there not been an agreement about their departure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, we'll analyse all these various elements in due course. What I'm asking you now is whether you're aware of the fact that the JNA left from Sarajevo, Tuzla, and other towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina which were not under the control of the Serbs. And then we'll come to Travnik and the specific conditions there. So that's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about it, having learnt about it subsequently. I didn't know about it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And I'd like us to clarify the conditions which you agreed upon with representatives of the JNA in Travnik for the withdrawal, and I'm going to ask you that because the Prosecutor put it to you or suggested an answer according to which the JNA was allowed to leave Travnik with their weapons, and you responded to that and said with side-arms, personal weapons. So I now feel that it's not quite clear what it was, in fact, that you agreed upon as being the conditions for the JNA's withdrawal. What were the soldiers allowed to take with them and what were they not?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't want to belittle the armed forces to which I had belonged just a few days earlier, so with their side-arms they left the Travnik Garrison with dignity. A Praga and a three-barrelled cannon could not be taken. The mortars that they had could not be taken, and any other larger weapons, larger than side-arms. And that, for officers, were pistols, and, for soldiers, were rifles. Now, for every 10 soldiers, one Zolja-type weapon, and nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, as far as this heavy weaponry is concerned that was left in the JNA barracks, what did you do with that?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We divided it up with the Muslims 50:50, and we divided up the barracks, everything else. The facilities and everything else was divided up on a 50:50 basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did anyone -- any of the soldiers or the Muslims [as interpreted] who were Muslims take part in your negotiations with representatives of the JNA about the withdrawal from the barracks?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Dzemal Merdan and Halid Genjac as the political leaders at the time that we conducted the negotiations about the withdrawal, and the president of the municipality. His name was Tamburic. So that was as far as the Muslim side was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. General, I think that that is all clear now. And now a few clarifications related to the meeting in Busovaca on the 16th of January, 1993, and the speech delivered by Dario Kordic. Yes, I meant to say "1992." I keep saying "3." So 1992 is the date. Now, let's all look at 4D2018, the next document, please. General, the document is in English, so focus on what I'm saying. I prepared it to make things clear and for us to be able to explain why there was such a lot of heated argument here in the courtroom last Thursday, and perhaps Mr. Scott wasn't clear where the problem lay. So, General, the Prosecutor asked you about Dario Kordic's speech, and he paraphrased Kordic's words. And then it was said that the Croatian people would not be part of any other Croatia. That word, "Croatia," led to a heated reaction because we were -- it was clear to us and we heard that Dario Kordic was speaking about a rump Yugoslavia. And now just to clear this matter up once and for all, all the misunderstandings that occurred: In the transcript from your testimony, Mr. Scott's question was recorded correctly, so Mr. Scott did not say "another Croatia," but he said "other creations," "any other creation" were the words he used, and so due to misunderstandings in the translation there was such heated reaction in the courtroom. So I just wanted us to clear that up. But tell us, General, on that day, the 16th of January, 1993 --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, 1992, sorry. Busovaca celebrated the international recognition of the Republic of Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, at that moment the Republic of Slovenia was also outside Yugoslavia; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So what did we call the remainder of Yugoslavia when Slovenia and Croatia had stepped down?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was referred to as the rump Yugoslavia. As far as I was concerned, it was no longer Yugoslavia at all, in no shape or form.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, to the best of your knowledge, what was your attitude and the attitude of the Croats that you knew about the -- about Bosnia-Herzegovina remaining in that kind of rump Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Impossible, inconceivable, unimaginable.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did they use the first opportunity offered to them, which was a referendum in this case, for Bosnia and Herzegovina to step down from the rump Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be an independent state?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. So did the Croatians take up that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, for you, at a time when Bosnia-Herzegovina gained its independence and international recognition, was it clear to you that the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as an independent state, could not be changed by force and could not be changed unless the international community allowed it?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without [as interpreted] recognition by the main powers in the world, the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina became inviolable, as they were everywhere; that is to say, the borders of the republics of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, General, let's discuss your testimony in the Kordic trial, when you spoke about Dario Kordic. The document is once again in English, so please concentrate on what I'm saying. The number is 4D2019, 4D2019. That's right. General, my colleague Mr. Scott put two paragraphs to you from the judgement in the Kordic case, the first-instance judgement, but it wasn't clear to us what those paragraphs referred to. If you will remember, they were paragraphs 585 and 586. Mr. Scott at the time put this to you. He said that the Trial Chamber in the Kordic trial did not lend you its trust and didn't take on board your position whereby Dario Kordic was not a military commander. Now, I want to show that the paragraphs which the Prosecution showed you related to the conflict in Busovaca in January 1993. And as to the conflict in Busovaca, you said in the Kordic trial, on page 17217 of the transcript, you said the following, and I'll read it out in English: [In English] "Are you really telling us that you had had no knowledge of any attack in Busovaca in late January 1993? "A. The attack on Busovaca, from what I knew, was launched by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Territorial Defence, with a view to taking position -- with a view to taking Busovaca. That was what I know about Busovaca." [Interpretation] Tell us, General -- as far as I've been able to see, that was all you said about the conflicts in Busovaca, when asked by the Prosecution, and this took place in January 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These questions linked to Kordic took me by surprise. I was surprised that the Trial Chamber had not taken into account my testimony, and that they were convicted, and they made me out to be dishonourable for having testified in the Kordic trial. What I'm afraid is that here, during this testimony, all my efforts to help the Trial Chamber in bringing about its decision are going to fall through, and I felt as if I was just a piece of paper sitting here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know, General. We'll clarify that, clear all that up later on, but through the facts I'm going to show that the Prosecution put forward an erroneous thesis and that -- and if you would allow me to continue, I wish to show that it was not correct, and I want to show what you actually said, and I want to show that the Trial Chamber in the Kordic trial, in actual fact, did adopt your position. What I want to put to you next is the following: In the appeals judgement, Kordic appeals judgement, the Chamber concluded or, in a way, confirmed the opinions of the first-instance judgement that Kordic was a political leader with military influence, and that, as such, he was involved in the planning and ordering of the crimes that are mentioned. And the crimes that are mentioned are the ones in Busovaca in January 1993. Now, linked to Dario Kordic as a politician, wielding a certain amount of military influence, I'm going to put your testimony forward about Blaskic. It is on page 17220 of the transcript from the Kordic trial. The Prosecution put a conversation to you between Blaskic and Kordic which was intercepted, and you commented on that and said that you don't believe that it was true and that it seemed to you to be somebody putting this in as an intercept. Anyway, I'm going to quote what you said, what your answer was, in English: [In English] "To begin with, I am not sure; that is, I don't know if that is a conversation between Blaskic and Kordic. If he has the authority, as you say, then it must have to do with the personal relationship between them." [Interpretation] Or, in other words, you, General, said that if Kordic could have suggested to Blaskic what he should do in a military sense, that it was a question governed by their personal relationships. Do you remember that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testified that the relationship between Kordic and Blaskic, Kiseljak/Busovaca, well, there could have been no contact like that, so that the transcript or whatever it was that I read, after the war in the paper "Slobodna Bosna," that it was construed in some way, fabricated. But what was authentic was the part where they swore, used swear words in their conversation, but that it wasn't realistic as to what was implied there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, the transcript reference is 47738. In this trial, you told us, and I'm going to provide a summary in Croatian, that Kordic could not exercise command in the Vitez recruitment area. He was in a position to exert influence over some of the commanders. He did have a certain charisma as well as power in certain situations, but I can also tell you as follows: He was in no position to exercise command in Travnik, Vitez, or, indeed, Novi Travnik. He could not issue orders in Zepce or Lozancic. He couldn't do anything in Kiseljak, in the Kiseljak area. He could not give orders to anyone. I think the remaining portion is not so relevant. General, do you allow for the possibility that Dario Kordic had a significant political influence over people in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did have political influence over people in Central Bosnia. He got them organised before the election, on the eve of the election and so on and so forth, so he did have a certain amount of influence, but he was not in command, nor indeed could he have been in command, nor indeed did he ever try to be in command. My impression of him as a soldier was that he was a bit like a fashion model, carrying no weapons at all. People were guarding him, but he was no commander, he wasn't the man who was headed straight into the thick of it, the fighting, or indeed anyone giving orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Another question, and then we'll go back to Kordic. General, when you say "commander," when you say "chain of command," who do you mean; a person who actually holds a rank as a military commander, and the chain construed as going from the top-ranking soldier, trickling down to lower-ranked soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Command" means that someone can and has the right to exercise command. He has some people below him, and those below him are under an obligation to carry out the other man's orders. That is what I would mean by "chain of command."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, what would you say about the following situation: We know that the HVO had brigades and that the brigades were more or less based on the existing municipalities. For example, a brigade commander attends a morning meeting or coffee on a daily basis. He goes to the president of the HVO in that particular municipality for that meeting. Other people are also there who hold certain offices in that municipality. The brigade commander likes to hear what the opinions are of the local civilian leader. He's inclined to act in keeping with the civilian leader's wishes. And now my question. This local leader, in your opinion, does he have a place in the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Command is one thing. Influence over commanders is a different thing. Grubesic could have got in touch with Kordic, or Blaskic could have got in touch with Kordic. They could have acted on that. But he was always the commander, Kordic, or Grubesic in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the hypothetical level as I first presented it. This would mean that the local civilian leader is not part of the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, he is not a part of that chain.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This fact, him not being a part of the chain of command, if that's what the circumstances were, does this change anything about the fact that the local political leader has effective power and that he may make suggestions to the commander as to what to do and what course of action should be taken?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has power. He has the power to influence certain developments. He proposes that something be done. He criticises the fact that a step was not taken or a measure was not taken. But we're still at the level of political influence. This does not constitute command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. In a bid to sum up the role of this local politician, would it, in your opinion, be fair to say that he is no military commander, he is not a part of the chain of command, but he does have power and he can exert influence on political developments in his municipality?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Take the example of Travnik. Mr. Tamburic blames me because the compound was taken or something. He has influence. He wields this influence and exerts pressure. He tries to get things his own way, to have things his own way, but he's in no position to order me to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us go back to Dario Kordic and everything that's been said about him so far. If my understanding of your evidence is correct, we could say, in relation to Dario Kordic, that he was no military commander, he was not a part of the chain of command, but he did have certain power, and he was in a position to influence certain military commanders; would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a lot of power and, yes, he was in a position to influence commanders by using his personal influence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now have a look at what the Appeals Chamber of this trial decided in the Kordic case about Kordic, himself. The Chamber did not conclude that he was a military commander or, indeed, a part of the chain of command; rather, it concluded that he was a political leader with a degree of military influence. Because of his de facto influence, he can be held responsible in relation to certain things that happened. My conclusion is that the Trial Chamber arrived at the exactly the same conclusion as you, general, about the possible role of a civilian official or, indeed, his influence on military commanders.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, they kept asking me questions about command, and I said he was not in command and he was in no position to be in command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, we need to draw a distinction between command, on the one hand, and external effective control over military commanders.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a commander. I set the notion of command quite apart from anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My next subject is about the organigram that the OTP showed you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Before counsel continues and just if I could have one brief intervention. I've been, I think, pretty good about not getting on my feet. Since a rather serious allegation is being made about my alleged mis-characterisation of the record, I just want to make the record clear, and I'm looking at the document that counsel has marked 4D02019. We've now, in the last some minutes, heard all sorts of things about Mr. Filipovic's further testimony in the Kordic case. However -- and if you look -- if you look at the right side of the page, down below the appeals judgement, there are references to a number of transcript references, starting with 17051. I waited, because I wanted to make sure I didn't jump the gun, to see what counsel -- if counsel would cover it, but I have to point out for the record that the one citation she doesn't deal with and hasn't dealt with this afternoon is the specific citation by the Kordic Trial Chamber. When you look at the left side of the page, what the Trial Chamber said was: "To this end, a great deal of evidence was called to show that Kordic played no military part in the conflict and simply wished to help his people. The Defence relies on this evidence in respect of Kordic's alleged role in the Busovaca conflict; footnote 1069." If we go to 1069 at the lower part of the page: "Many witnesses gave evidence of this, including military commands and others; Major General Filip Filipovic at transcript page 17045." Not a page that counsel has dealt with on the right side of the page. And at P -- and at transcript page 17045, the citation given by the Trial Chamber -- the Kordic Trial Chamber and which the Kordic Trial Chamber rejected was his -- this testimony of the witness. I said that Mr. Kordic never had command over any military unit in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. That's exactly what was cited by the Kordic Trial Chamber, and not these other items on the page. I simply want the record to be clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there's no need to interpret this. I understand my learned friend Mr. Scott would want something like this to appear on the record, but it's perfectly clear that there is not a single statement by General Filipovic here about the clashes in Busovaca in January 1993 that might back or corroborate what my learned friend is saying. I do think this is crystal clear. Anyway, therefore, I shall not dwell on it any longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, we spoke about this organigram used by General Petkovic in the Blaskic case. This is P11123. As we're waiting for the document to come up on our screens, I would like to point out that the English translation of this document is insufficient in one particularly important aspect. The link between the commander-in-chief and the Main Staff is missing, and it is a direct link which bypasses the Defence Department. There is a link between the commander-in-chief and the Main Staff. The Croatian document shows that very clearly. In the English document, the link is missing. Therefore, I think it should be corrected, because it just might prove very important further down the road in this case. General, you were asked something about re-subordination in relation to this document. Among other questions, you were asked who you would report to or who you would get in touch, for example, with in your Travnik Brigade if you wanted an element of the Convicts Battalion to come out and help you. The Convicts Battalion, if we look at this chart, is only linked to the commander-in-chief, and no one else?
