You said that in a technical sense, you would send a request by packet communications or a different type of equipment, you would send it on through to the Main Staff. Judge Antonetti then went on to state: "Therefore, it would be natural for you to go through the Main Staff to achieve this." My question for you, General: If the Convicts Battalion was only subordinated to the commander-in-chief of the HVO and no one else, who, then, would have had the power to make a decision regarding the re-subordination of a component unit of the Convicts Battalion, for example, to the Vitez operations area?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it would never have occurred to me, never have crossed my mind, to ask for the assistance of the Convicts Battalion. But if I'd needed the services of another unit holding the same position as the Convicts Battalion, again, technically, I would have gone through the Main Staff. Who could the decision have been taken by, as the chart shows; by the command-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, General, that's quite sufficient for my purposes. Now a very brief question about today's evidence. There was a brief mention of men fit for military service. There was a short document bearing the name of General Petkovic. It was said that those men should be kept in Sovici and Doljani. My question, General: Were these men fit for military service under a military obligation?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At a time of war, these military conscripts, are they active forces or reserve forces? Do they actively contribute to the defence of their countries or are they considered to be civilians?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina or in the area in which I happened to be, everyone was a military conscript. And they could be assigned to a civilian posts as well, but the military duty was incumbent equally upon everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If they weren't assigned to some sort of work assignment or something else, such as a post in the Civilian Protection, they were an active service army; right?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they belonged to one of the units in the active service.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You were asked today, General, what you, as a military commander, would have done had one of your soldiers set fire to a house or, indeed, committed any sort of criminal offence. You said you would have had them detained. General, your answer assumes that you actually know who the perpetrator was, who set fire to a house or who committed a crime. I'm asking you now: In your capacity as a military commander, would you have launched an investigation in a situation in which the perpetrator remained unknown, you don't know who it was who set fire to a house or committed a crime?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we talk about taking measures, we assume that the measures will be effective, that my life is not at risk in any way. When Dzemal Merdan came to the village of Jelinak with us, the commission and the command, finding the same sort of situation that probably prevailed in Santici or Ahmici, we see soldiers there setting fire to houses, we see dead bodies. The people involved are attacking Dzemal Merdan, and had the Cheshire Battalion soldiers not protected him, they would have killed him. What could a commanding officer possibly do in a situation like that? When Dzemal Merdan, a high-ranking BH Army officer, said, What on earth are you doing, we have the international community here, they attacked him with rifles. And had it not been for him being protected by the British Battalion, they would have killed him. This gives you an idea of what a high-ranking or low-ranking military officer can do, and this idea is necessarily a relative one because it relates to what is actually going on and what actually went on in my area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you anything about the actual possibilities, but what somebody's duty-bound to do.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are duty-bound to prevent something which is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, quickly, because I would like your testimony to end today - we have 20 minutes left and still some topics to broach - but, quickly, I'm just hearing about what happened with Mr. Merdan, where soldiers wanted to kill him, and he was fortunately saved by the intervention of the BritBat. Well, that's fine, but while I was listening to you, I was thinking about the rebellion in 1917 where rogue soldiers had decided not to go and fight during World War I, and generals at that time, just like generals like you, had decided to set up martial courts and to try these soldiers, and then execute them immediately. Couldn't you set up a martial court and try these soldiers that were attacking Mr. Merdan, under your very own eyes and the eyes of the international community? Weren't you able to do that? Didn't you have the competence to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Impossible, impossible, to set up a court-martial, nor was there any court-martial in Bosnia-Herzegovina as far as I know. What you could perhaps do was to engage the Intervention Platoon which was more under the control of a commander, or the military police if it was further away from the front, because the military police is not up at the front. So at a later stage, once the soldier was no longer at the place where the event had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, tell us, please, whose soldiers tried to kill Mr. Merdan?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the Territorial Defence, I think those of the 7th Muslim Brigade -- as I was saying, members of the Territorial Defence cleansed the village of Jelinak, and we came to solve the issue, and that was that particular event.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, a brief explanation about some documents particularly with respect to Mr. Roso and Blaskic, dating to May 1992, with the subject of the HVO being the only legal entity, now which one of the two was legal, the HVO or the BH Army, or whatever. Now, the Prosecutor showed you a series of documents ending with one dated the 11th of May dealing with that subject. If you go back to the agreement about friendship and co-operation, think back, which on the 21st of July, 1992, was signed by Alija Izetbegovic and Franjo Tudjman, which is document P339, my question to you is this: In that document, for the first time it says loud and clear that the HVO and the BH Army are equally components of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, my question to you is this, General: To the best of your knowledge, any time afterwards, as presented by the Prosecution, as put to you by the Prosecution, was there a discussion about whether the HVO was the legal and legitimate military force of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but also of the Muslims and everybody else who wished to take part in combat?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that was in July 1992. That particular agreement was a correct and proper agreement, as far as the situation on the ground was concerned, although at the same time there were attempts to do things beyond -- that went beyond this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now a brief question, General, just to avoid any misunderstanding. My colleague Mr. Scott put it to you -- or, rather, suggested an answer to this effect: that the HVO was an organised and significant military force in 1992, at the end of 1992, in actual fact. And that is on transcript page 47696 -- 46696 [as interpreted]. And you went on to explain that there was a difference in relation to April 1992. So I want to ask you something now linked to a portion of your testimony in the Kordic trial, recorded on page 17017 of the transcript, where you say that there wasn't enough time to establish full military organisation and that you -- one needed some time in peace and then another year or two in order to establish an army in the proper sense of the word, a real army. Now, to the best of your knowledge, General, what would you say? When did the HVO become an organised army capable of carrying out attack and defence assignments which could be considered organised in the sense of a professional modern army?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had an army, and I've already said that, only as of 1994, and just a part of an army, in actual fact, because we had guards brigades that were being established, and there were manoeuvre units, and you could go on assignment with the proper unit only in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Filipovic, one of the ways in which the Prosecution attempted to shake the Trial Chamber's trust and confidence in your testimony was your alleged statement to the HINA agency with respect to the indictment raised against the six Croats from Central Bosnia. To the best of your recollection, the first indictments that were raised by the Prosecution of this Tribunal against Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina were exclusively from Central Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only Croats, but the first 20 indictments -- within the first 20 indictments, there were 15 indictments against Croats, and that was quite surprising and astonishing when I realised that. And when you look at the number of years people were sentenced to, terms of imprisonment, that was quite astounding, too; at least it was to me, because as I said, we put up a pure defence, a crime had been committed. Unfortunately, in my state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were a lot of crimes committed by Muslim, Serbs, and Croats, crimes to each other and, especially, victims on the part from the international community that had come to help out the country, help my country out, and they ended up losing their lives, they were killed or they were belittled or whatever. And so in that sense, the Lasva Valley could not have been the centre of these negative events that took place within this country of mine that was Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, you started answering a question of mine, and I said we'll deal with that in due course. So to wind up now, Mr. Scott tried to compromise you as a witness by saying that you were a Defence witness for Dario Kordic in the trial -- in the Kordic trial held at this Tribunal. Tell me, General, what do you think about that? What do you think about it, when a Defence witness -- when they try to discredit a witness merely through the fact of his being a witness for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a terrible message, a message sent out, that a witness testified in a case when the accused stood trial and were found guilty. That's a terrible message. It's something that I was really shaken to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. I'm sorry, but I'm not going to allow --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we allow the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm not going to allow my --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... finish the answer. The witness didn't finish the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: He did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, then I'll wait. Then I will wait. But, I do want to address the matter. That's -- that statement against me cannot simply be allowed to stand. That was not our position, that was never my position, but I'll let the witness answer first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Witness, how did you experience this and what did you think?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my overall impressions from that is that part of this Tribunal, the Prosecution sees his work --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer? Could the witness be asked to repeat his answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Repeat that, General, please, for the record. It wasn't recorded. The interpreters didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This Tribunal -- well, the witness is lost in all the cacophony of voices, procedure, and so on. I said that the Prosecution is Caesar's wife; she cannot be thought to do wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: "Caesar's wife." "Caesar," C-a-e --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, what did you have to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Well, first of all on the last point, I've never known anyone in this institution to be the slightest bit reluctant to criticise the Prosecution for anything, and so I don't know anything about being Caesar's wife, but that's not been my experience. Secondly, Your Honour, that mis-characterises -- more importantly, that mis-characterises the Prosecution's position, in particular my position. I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me. I never took the position, I have never taken the position, I don't expect to ever take the position, that a witness's testimony should be questioned simply because he or she came to testify for the Defence. That is not my position. I raise a separate, different issue in terms of the nature of his specific testimony in the Kordic case, the evidence that he was confronted with to the contrary, and the Trial Chamber's assessment of his evidence. I have never taken the position, I will never take the position, that a witness should be adjudged less credible simply because he was called for one side or the other. And to characterise my position as that is not correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And my final question: Witness, if you remember, Mr. Scott said that you had testified for Dario Kordic and that you considered Dario Kordic to be a hero. You tried to explain to him that as far as you were concerned, for you Dario Kordic was not a hero, and you tried to explain why you agreed to be a witness for Dario Kordic's Defence, but you weren't able to finish your thoughts. So tell us now, in your opinion, as far as you're concerned, is Dario Kordic a hero, and why did you go to testify for Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the Kordic trial, in this particular trial, and when Alagic was accused, I offered to come forward and testify because I lived during the time when all that was going on, and I wanted to assist the Court in uncovering the truth and making their serious decision. Now, Kordic, a hero? Well, he cannot be a hero, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And my last question, General, is this: Tell us, please, in your opinion, as far as you're concerned, at any time during the conflict with the BH Army was the dilemma with -- was there a dilemma whether you were defending Bosnia-Herzegovina or not?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, all my efforts, before and now, were for Bosnia-Herzegovina. I did not defend Bosnia-Herzegovina in some imagined or recognised form, but as life and civilisation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think that was my duty, because I was a professional. Now, I could have pulled out. I had a way of not being involved. But from one day to the next, I was engaged in the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General Filipovic. And that concludes my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, your testimony is now over. I would like to thank you, on behalf of my fellow Judges and myself, to have come here to The Hague for the Defence of General Petkovic and to help us elicit the truth. I wish you the best and a safe return home, and I will ask our usher to please escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I be allowed to say something briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, if you want to tell us -- to ask us whether we heard you, fine. But if you want to make speeches on this trial, this is not the right forum for this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was always greeted, both by the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber in the Tribunal. I would like to say thank you to the Tribunal for giving me the opportunity of giving you my visions of the problems that my country faced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, I hope the witness is ready for tomorrow morning. Is everything okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness was already here in court, but we sent him back to his hotel. But, yes, he is ready and will appear tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Kovacic, is Mr. Praljak ill? Why is he not with us in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak is tired. I can't say he is sick. He's just tired and said he'd prefer not to come in. He says he's not feeling very well, so that's why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We hope that he will soon get better and we'll have him in the courtroom tomorrow. I thank you all. Have a pleasant evening, and we'll resume tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 8th day of December, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.57 p.m.,
